options: Cortical region of the adrenal gland
mcqs.why: Aldosterone is secreted from the cortical region of the adrenal gland and helps in the reabsorption of sodium; the book also lists insulin from the pancreas as helping to reabsorb glucose from the glomerular filtrate.

lessons.title: Disorders of Urinary Tract: UTI, Kidney Stones, Kidney Failure, Dialysis and Transplant
lessons.notes_html:
The urinary tract includes kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra. Its disorders include urinary tract infections, kidney stones, kidney failure, bladder control problems and prostate problems. Some last only for a short time while others are long lasting. The branch of medical science which deals with urinary tract disorders and treatment is urology.

15.5 Disorders of Urinary Tract

15.5.1 Urinary Tract Infections (UTI)

Infections that affect any part of the urinary tract are called urinary tract infections (UTI). They are more virulent in females than males because of the shorter urethra in women, incomplete emptying of the bladder, and the large exposed surface area of the external genitalia. Ureters are less infected as compared to other parts of the urinary tract due to their acidic nature. Infection of the upper urinary tract is known as pyelonephritis (e.g. kidney infection); infection of the lower tract is cystitis (e.g. infection of the bladder).

The most common cause of infection is Escherichia coli; other bacteria, viruses and fungi may also cause UTI. Sexual contact with infected partners and unhygienic conditions are the major causes of UTI. Symptoms may include a burning feeling during urination, cloudy, dark or bloody urine or strange smelling urine, feeling tired, fever or chill. Treatment: antibiotics as prescribed, and drinking more water to flush out pathogens.

15.5.2 Kidney Stones (Nephrolithiasis)

The hard mineralized material that clings together and forms pebbles within the kidney or any other part of the urinary tract, like the ureter or bladder, is called a kidney stone. Stones are small, about 2–3 mm in diameter, and one to many in number; very small stones may pass out without symptoms. Symptoms may include pain while urinating, blood in urine, sharp pain in the back and lower abdomen, nausea and vomiting. Calcium stones are the most common type, usually made of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate. Uric acid stones form when urine is often too acidic; uric acid can form a stone by itself or by mixing with calcium.

Treatment depends on the size, composition and location of the stone, traced by x-ray, CT scan, blood test and urine test. Small stones are usually treated with medicine, but large and complex stones usually need surgery or lithotripsy.

Lithotripsy is a medical procedure involving the physical destruction of hardened masses like kidney stones, bezoars or gallstones; the term is derived from Greek words meaning breaking (or pulverizing) stones. Its two types are:

  • Extracorporeal Shock Wave lithotripsy — Shock waves break the kidney stones into small pieces, which then pass through the urinary tract and out of the body. The treatment usually takes 45 minutes to one hour and may be done under general anaesthesia so the patient does not feel pain.
  • Laser lithotripsy — By ureteroscopy, in which a long tube-shaped tool is used to find, remove and break the stone; a laser breaks the stone into small pieces so they may pass through the urinary tract.

15.5.3 Kidney Failure

Kidney failure, also called end-stage renal disease (ESRD), is the last stage of chronic kidney disease: the kidneys are not working well enough for the survival of the patient without dialysis or a kidney transplant. Factors related to kidney failure include autoimmune diseases, kidney stones, diabetes, high blood pressure, use of drugs and bacterial infections. Diabetes is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease (44%), followed by high blood pressure (28%). Symptoms include nausea and vomiting, muscle cramps, appetite loss, swelling in feet and ankles, too much urine and sleeplessness. Acute kidney failure is usually caused by injuries, vomiting, diarrhoea, water shortage from excessive sweating or diuresis, ureter blockage by a stone, and severe nephritis. The few options for kidney failure patients are the types of dialysis and kidney transplant.

15.5.4 Dialysis

Dialysis is the temporary treatment for kidney failure patients, in which toxins and wastes are removed from the body by artificial means, i.e. using dialyzing fluid. It is not a permanent cure for kidney disease.

  • Hemodialysis — The most common type. It uses an artificial kidney (hemodialyzer) to remove wastes, toxins and extra fluids from the blood. Blood passes through sterile tubing to a filter in the machine, via a gortex graft between an artery and a vein in the arm or leg, or a direct artery–vein connection (cimino fistula); a solution on the other side of the filter receives the wastes, and the cleaned blood returns to the patient.
  • Peritoneal dialysis — Uses the lining of the abdomen, the peritoneum, to filter blood. A catheter is placed near the navel a few weeks before treatment starts; the patient can do this dialysis himself. Dialysis solution (water with salt and other additives) is transferred from a bag into the peritoneal cavity, where it soaks up wastes and extra fluids; after a few hours the fluid, filled with waste, drains out into a separate bag and fresh fluid is entered. This process is called an exchange.

15.5.5 Kidney Transplant: Process and Problems

Kidney transplant is a surgical procedure of placing a healthy donor kidney into the belly of a chronic kidney failure patient. Transplantation is the preferred treatment over dialysis, as it improves and normalizes the life of the patient. The kidney may come from a deceased organ donor or from a living donor (living transplant); the living donor can live a healthy life with a single kidney. Before transplant, the tissue type of donor and recipient is matched. The operation takes 3–4 hours; usually one kidney is given, the affected kidney is left in place, and the new kidney is placed in the lower belly and attached to a large artery, starting to clean the blood as soon as it is connected. The first kidney transplant was done in Boston by Joseph E. Murray in 1954.

Problems: a kidney transplant is a major operation, with complications such as pain, delayed wound healing, bleeding and risk of infection. However, kidney rejection is the most serious problem. Medication like cyclosporine is given to suppress the immune system of the recipient to prevent rejection of the transplant kidney.

Key Points

  • UTI is most commonly caused by Escherichia coli; upper tract infection is pyelonephritis, lower tract infection is cystitis.
  • Kidney stones are hard pebbles about 2–3 mm; calcium stones are most common, uric acid stones form in acidic urine.
  • Lithotripsy breaks stones: extracorporeal shock wave (45 minutes to one hour) and laser lithotripsy by ureteroscopy.
  • Kidney failure (ESRD) needs dialysis or transplant; diabetes (44%) and high blood pressure (28%) are its leading causes.
  • Hemodialysis uses a hemodialyzer; peritoneal dialysis uses the peritoneum and peritoneal cavity in exchanges.
  • In transplant, rejection is the most serious problem and cyclosporine is given to prevent it.

mcqs.q: The branch of medical science dealing with urinary tract disorders and treatment is called:
mcqs.why: The notes state the branch of medical science which deals with urinary tract disorders and treatment is urology, while nephrology is the study of the structure, functions and diseases of the kidney.

mcqs.q: Infection of the upper urinary tract is known as pyelonephritis, while infection of the lower tract, such as the bladder, is:
mcqs.why: Infection of the upper urinary tract is pyelonephritis (e.g. kidney infection); infection of the lower tract is cystitis (e.g. infection of the bladder). Ureters are less infected due to their acidic nature.

mcqs.q: The most common cause of urinary tract infection is:
mcqs.why: The most common cause of UTI is Escherichia coli; other bacteria, viruses and fungi may also cause it, and UTI is more virulent in females because of the shorter urethra.

mcqs.q: Kidney stones are hard pebbles within the kidney or urinary tract, typically about:
mcqs.why: Kidney stones (nephrolithiasis) are hard mineralized material forming pebbles; stones are small, about 2-3 mm in diameter, one to many in number, and very small stones may pass without symptoms.

mcqs.q: The most common type of kidney stone is:
options: Uric acid stones, formed in acidic urine
Calcium stones, usually made of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate
Chloride stones from the chloride shift
mcqs.why: Calcium stones are the most common type, usually made of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate; uric acid stones form when urine is often too acidic.

mcqs.q: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy treats kidney stones by:
options: Using a laser through a ureteroscope
Using shock waves to break stones into small pieces that pass out, usually taking 45 minutes to one hour
mcqs.why: In extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy, shock waves break kidney stones into small pieces which pass through the urinary tract; treatment usually takes 45 minutes to one hour and may be under general anaesthesia.

mcqs.q: Diabetes accounts for 44 percent and high blood pressure for 28 percent of chronic kidney disease. Together they account for:
mcqs.why: Working: 44 + 28 = 72 percent. The notes state diabetes is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease (44 percent), followed by high blood pressure (28 percent).

mcqs.q: In hemodialysis, wastes are removed from blood using:
options: An artificial kidney (hemodialyzer), where blood passes through sterile tubing to a filter in the machine
A catheter near the navel only
mcqs.why: Hemodialysis is the most common type of dialysis; it uses an artificial kidney (hemodialyzer) to remove wastes, toxins and extra fluids, via a gortex graft or cimino fistula, and cleaned blood returns to the patient.

mcqs.q: Peritoneal dialysis differs from hemodialysis because it:
options: Uses the lining of the abdomen, the peritoneum, to filter blood, with solution exchanged through a catheter near the navel
Uses an external machine for all filtration
mcqs.why: Peritoneal dialysis uses the peritoneum to filter blood; dialysis solution enters the peritoneal cavity through a catheter near the navel, soaks up wastes, and drains out in a process called an exchange.

mcqs.q: In kidney transplant, the most serious problem is rejection, prevented by giving:
options: Cyclosporine to suppress the immune system of the recipient
mcqs.why: Kidney rejection is the most serious problem of transplant; medication like cyclosporine is given to suppress the immune system of the recipient to prevent rejection of the transplant kidney.

lessons.title: Thermoregulation: Classification of Animals and Strategies in Man
lessons.notes_html:
Thermoregulation is the maintenance of internal body temperature at a nearly constant state so that the body can perform its metabolic activities at the optimum level. Any change in temperature will affect enzyme activity, and thus metabolic reactions will be disturbed.

15.6 Thermoregulation

15.6.1 Classification of Animals on the Basis of Temperature (Thermoregulation)

On the basis of temperature regulation, animals can be divided into two groups:

  • Poikilotherms — Animals not able to regulate their internal body temperature; they depend on an external source of heat (sunlight) to get themselves warm, and their body temperature changes with the external temperature. They have to hibernate in low temperature and aestivate (summer sleep) in high temperature. These include fish, amphibians and reptiles.
  • Homeotherms — Animals able to regulate their internal body temperature, not dependent on an external source of heat. They have a high metabolic rate and need more food to generate heat in their body. These include birds and mammals.

On the basis of heat production, animals can be divided into three categories:

  • Ectotherms — Generate metabolic heat at a low level due to a low metabolic rate, so they depend on an external source of heat for their survival. These include insects, fish, amphibians and reptiles.
  • Endotherms — Can generate enough heat to maintain their body temperature due to a high metabolic rate, and can survive in all sorts of habitats. These include birds and mammals. They generate their own body heat through heat production as a by-product of metabolism.
  • Heterotherms — Animals with a thermoregulatory strategy intermediate to ectotherms and endotherms: they produce heat in their body but also depend on an external source of heat. These include small mammals like the bat and small birds like the humming bird.
GroupMeaningExamples
PoikilothermsCannot regulate internal temperature; it changes with the environmentFish, amphibians, reptiles
HomeothermsRegulate internal temperature; high metabolic rateBirds, mammals
EctothermsLow metabolic heat; depend on external heatInsects, fish, amphibians, reptiles
EndothermsGenerate enough metabolic heat to maintain temperatureBirds, mammals
HeterothermsIntermediate: produce heat and also use external heatBat, humming bird

15.6.2 Thermoregulatory Strategies in Man

The body temperature of man is regulated and stabilized by the hypothalamus, a region of the brain basically concerned with homeostasis — it works as a complex homeostatic thermostat. In case of any variation in the set point, endocrine production initiates a control mechanism to increase or decrease energy production or dissipation, to return the temperature towards the set point.

During hot (hyperthermia) conditions — hyperthermia is increased body temperature:

  • Vasodilation, i.e. expansion of blood capillaries under the skin, so that more heat can be brought towards the skin for dissipation of heat.
  • Activation of sweat glands.
  • Relaxation of hair erector muscles.

During cold (hypothermia) conditions, to prevent heat loss and generate heat:

  • Inactivation of sweat glands.
  • Vasoconstriction.
  • Increase in metabolic activities.
  • Shivering may start.
  • Brown fats are consumed for more and rapid heat production.

Science, Technology and Society (STS)

Kidney donation: recipients of a living donor kidney usually live a longer, healthier life compared to those who receive a deceased donor kidney, and there can be benefit to the donor as well, such as saving the life of another person and a greater understanding of one's own health. Transplant centres: the book names Shifa International Hospital, the Kidney Transplant Program of Aga Khan University Hospital and Kidney Transplant Doctors Hospital and Medical Centre Lahore; the Sindh Institute of Urology and Transplantation (SIUT), established by Dr. Adeeb Rizvi in 1971, is the most prominent and pioneer institute in Pakistan, and in Balochistan the Balochistan Institute of Nephrology, Urology Quetta (BINUQ) is named.

Key Points

  • Thermoregulation keeps body temperature nearly constant so enzymes and metabolism work at their optimum.
  • Poikilotherms cannot regulate temperature (fish, amphibians, reptiles); homeotherms can (birds, mammals).
  • By heat production: ectotherms depend on external heat, endotherms generate enough metabolic heat, heterotherms (bat, humming bird) are intermediate.
  • In man the hypothalamus is the thermostat for body temperature.
  • In heat: vasodilation, sweating and relaxation of hair erector muscles lose heat.
  • In cold: vasoconstriction, stopped sweating, increased metabolism, shivering and brown fat use produce and conserve heat.

mcqs.q: Poikilotherms, such as fish, amphibians and reptiles, are animals that:
options: Regulate internal temperature with a high metabolic rate
Cannot regulate their internal body temperature, which changes with the external temperature
Generate enough metabolic heat in all habitats
Are intermediate between ectotherms and endotherms
mcqs.why: Poikilotherms are not able to regulate their internal body temperature; they depend on external heat (sunlight), hibernate in low temperature and aestivate in high temperature. Examples are fish, amphibians and reptiles.

mcqs.q: Homeotherms, which include birds and mammals, are animals that:
options: Depend entirely on sunlight to warm up
Can regulate their internal body temperature and have a high metabolic rate, needing more food to generate heat
Produce no metabolic heat at all
mcqs.why: Homeotherms are able to regulate their internal body temperature, not dependent on an external source of heat; they have a high metabolic rate and need more food to generate heat. Birds and mammals are homeotherms.

mcqs.q: Ectotherms are defined on the basis of heat production as animals that:
options: Generate metabolic heat at a low level due to a low metabolic rate, so they depend on an external source of heat
Generate enough heat to maintain temperature in all habitats
Use brown fats for rapid heat production
mcqs.why: Ectotherms generate metabolic heat at a low level due to a low metabolic rate, so they depend on an external source of heat for survival; they include insects, fish, amphibians and reptiles.

mcqs.q: Heterotherms, intermediate between ectotherms and endotherms, include examples such as:
options: The bat and the humming bird
mcqs.why: Heterotherms produce heat in their body but also depend on an external source of heat; examples given are small mammals like the bat and small birds like the humming bird.

mcqs.q: In man, body temperature is regulated and stabilized by which region of the brain, acting as a thermostat?
options: The hypothalamus, a region basically concerned with homeostasis
mcqs.why: The body temperature of man is regulated and stabilized by the hypothalamus, a region of the brain basically concerned with homeostasis - it works as a complex homeostatic thermostat.

mcqs.q: During hot conditions (hyperthermia), heat is lost from the body by:
options: Vasodilation, activation of sweat glands and relaxation of hair erector muscles
Increased metabolic activities and brown fat use
mcqs.why: In hot conditions there is vasodilation, expanding capillaries under the skin to bring heat to the surface, activation of sweat glands, and relaxation of hair erector muscles, so heat is dissipated.

mcqs.q: During cold conditions (hypothermia), the body conserves and produces heat by:
options: Inactivation of sweat glands, vasoconstriction, increased metabolic activities, shivering and consumption of brown fats
Opening capillaries under the skin widely
mcqs.why: In cold: sweat glands are inactivated, vasoconstriction occurs, metabolic activities increase, shivering may start, and brown fats are consumed for more and rapid heat production.

mcqs.q: Thermoregulation is important because any change in temperature will affect:
options: Enzyme activity, and thus metabolic reactions will be disturbed
Only the colour of the skin
mcqs.why: Thermoregulation maintains internal body temperature at a nearly constant state so metabolic activities perform at the optimum level; any change in temperature will affect enzyme activity and disturb metabolic reactions.

mcqs.q: Endotherms, such as birds and mammals, can survive in all sorts of habitats because they:
options: Depend on external heat for survival
Can generate enough heat to maintain their body temperature due to a high metabolic rate
mcqs.why: Endotherms generate enough heat to maintain body temperature due to a high metabolic rate, generating body heat as a by-product of metabolism, and can survive in all sorts of habitats.

mcqs.q: According to the STS notes, the Sindh Institute of Urology and Transplantation (SIUT), the pioneer institute in Pakistan, was established by Dr Adeeb Rizvi in:
mcqs.why: The STS notes name SIUT, established by Dr Adeeb Rizvi in 1971, as the most prominent and pioneer institute in Pakistan for kidney transplant, alongside centres such as Shifa International and Aga Khan University Hospital.

lessons.title: Bone: Structure, Bone Cells and Cartilage
lessons.notes_html:
Movement is a change in shape or position of body parts; in locomotion the whole organism moves from one place to another. In animals movement is provided by muscles, while support gives the body its proper shape and structure. Support is provided by hydrostatic skeletons, bones and cartilages. The skeletal tissues are bone and cartilage.

16.1 Human Skeleton

The human skeleton is the main supportive framework of the body. It mainly includes bones and cartilages, and muscles are attached to it for effective movement. Bone is a connective tissue impregnated with calcium salts. It is hard, provides support, protects internal organs and gives an environment for the production of blood cells. The protein component of skeletal tissue is collagen.

16.1.1 Structure of Bone

Bone tissue is of two types: compact (hard and dense) bone outside and cancellous (spongy) bone inside.

  • Compact bone, also called cortical bone, is hard white tissue surrounding all bones. Its fundamental units are osteons or Haversian systems: concentric layers called lamellae around a central (Haversian) canal containing blood and nerve supply. The central canal communicates with the perforating (Volkmann's) canal, which transmits vessels from the periosteum (dense vascular connective tissue enveloping the bone) into the endosteum (thin layer lining the medullary cavity).
  • Osteocytes lie in small cavities called lacunae between the lamellae. Canaliculi are microscopic channels that transport nutrients to the osteocytes and remove their wastes.
  • Spongy bone, also called cancellous or trabecular bone, is porous and highly vascular, mostly at the ends of long bones. Its lacunae lie in a lattice-like network of matrix spikes called trabeculae, with osteocytes irregularly placed within them. The spaces make it lighter and less dense than compact bone and contain red bone marrow, where blood cells are formed.

An osteon: concentric lamellae around a central canal carrying blood vessels and nerves.

Types of Bone Cells

Bone growth and repair are carried out by four types of cells:

  • Osteogenic cells — Undifferentiated stem cells in the cellular layer of endosteum and periosteum; they divide and develop into osteoblasts.
  • Osteoblasts — Bone-forming cells, mostly where bone growth occurs; they secrete collagen and the bone matrix and cause its mineralization.
  • Osteocytes — Mature bone cells entrapped in the matrix (osteoblasts surrounded by matrix become osteocytes); by secreting enzymes they maintain the mineral concentration of the matrix.
  • Osteoclasts — Large, multinucleated bone-breaking (bone-resorbing) cells at sites of old, injured bone, derived from monocytes and macrophages.

About 10% of bone is replaced every year, so we get a new skeleton about every ten years.

16.1.2 Cartilage

Cartilage is a connective tissue composed of cells called chondrocytes and fibres embedded in a firm, gel-like matrix. It is much more elastic than bone and is found at joints and between bones, e.g. at the elbow, knees and ankles. It has no blood vessels or lymphatics and no nerves, so it is insensitive; nutrition diffuses through the matrix. It is surrounded by a fibrous membrane, the perichondrium. When cartilage calcifies, the chondrocytes die and it is replaced by bone-like tissue.

BoneCartilage
Hard; cells are osteocytesSoft; cells are chondrocytes
Matrix inflexible, with calcium saltsMatrix flexible, calcium salts absent
Rich blood supply; vascular; bone marrow presentNo blood supply; non-vascular; bone marrow absent
Outer covering is periosteumOuter covering is perichondrium
Provides skeletal supportProvides flexibility

Key Points

  • Skeletal tissues are bone and cartilage; bone is impregnated with calcium salts and its protein is collagen.
  • Compact bone is built of osteons (lamellae around a central canal); spongy bone is built of trabeculae and holds red bone marrow.
  • Osteogenic cells divide, osteoblasts form bone, osteocytes maintain it and osteoclasts break it down.
  • Cartilage is made of chondrocytes in a gel-like matrix; it is avascular, without nerves, and covered by perichondrium.
  • Osteocytes lie in lacunae; canaliculi carry nutrients to them.

mcqs.q: What is locomotion, as distinct from movement in general?
options: The whole organism moving from one place to another
A change in the shape of a body part only
The beating of cilia inside a body cavity
The contraction of a single muscle fibre
mcqs.why: The notes define movement as a change in shape or position of body parts, while in locomotion the whole organism moves from one place to another.

mcqs.q: Which protein is the protein component of skeletal tissue?
mcqs.why: Bone is a connective tissue impregnated with calcium salts, and the notes state that the protein component of skeletal tissue is collagen.

mcqs.q: The fundamental units of compact bone are called:
mcqs.why: Compact bone is built of osteons, also called Haversian systems, which are concentric lamellae arranged around a central Haversian canal.

mcqs.q: Osteocytes lie in small cavities between the lamellae called:
mcqs.why: The notes state that osteocytes lie in small cavities called lacunae between the lamellae, while canaliculi are the microscopic channels serving them.

mcqs.q: Which bone cells are large, multinucleated and break down old or injured bone?
mcqs.why: Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated bone-resorbing cells found at sites of old, injured bone, and they are derived from monocytes and macrophages.

mcqs.q: About what percentage of bone is replaced every year?
mcqs.why: The notes state that about 10 percent of bone is replaced every year, so a person gets a new skeleton about every ten years.

mcqs.q: Red bone marrow, where blood cells are formed, is found in:
mcqs.why: Spongy bone is porous and its spaces contain red bone marrow, where blood cells are formed, which is why it is highly vascular tissue.

mcqs.q: Which statement about cartilage is correct?
options: It has a rich blood supply and many nerves
It is covered by the periosteum
Its matrix contains abundant calcium salts
It has no blood vessels, lymphatics or nerves, so it is insensitive
mcqs.why: Cartilage has no blood vessels or lymphatics and no nerves, so it is insensitive, and its nutrition diffuses through its gel-like matrix.

mcqs.q: The perforating canal that transmits vessels from the periosteum into the endosteum is:
mcqs.why: The central canal communicates with the perforating Volkmann canal, which transmits vessels from the periosteum into the endosteum lining the medullary cavity.

mcqs.q: When cartilage calcifies, what happens to its chondrocytes?
options: They die and the cartilage is replaced by bone-like tissue
They turn into osteocytes at once
mcqs.why: The notes state that when cartilage calcifies, the chondrocytes die and the cartilage is replaced by bone-like tissue.

lessons.title: Functions of the Skeleton and the Axial Skeleton
lessons.notes_html:
The human skeleton is an endoskeleton: it lies inside the organism with muscles attached outside, and it is made of living tissues that grow with the organism.

16.1.3 Functions of Human Skeleton

  • It gives support to the body; without it the body would be flabby and shapeless.
  • It protects internal organs, e.g. the skull protects the brain and the rib cage protects the heart and lungs.
  • It provides a surface for the attachment of muscles, ligaments and tendons, and bones act as levers for movement; bones and joints work with muscles so we can walk and run.
  • It stores 97% of the body calcium and phosphorus (mineral storage).
  • Blood cells are made in red bone marrow, mostly present in the ribs and limb bones.

Divisions of Human Skeleton

The human skeleton of 206 bones is divided into the axial skeleton of 80 bones and the appendicular skeleton of 126 bones. The axial skeleton is mostly fused; the appendicular skeleton is unfused and consists of girdles and limbs. Hands and feet alone contain 106 bones: each hand has 27 bones and each foot 26 bones.

Axial Skeleton: Skull

The axial skeleton includes the skull (cranium and facial bones), hyoid bone, vertebral column, sternum and ribs. The cranium is a bony cavity that contains and protects the brain. It has 8 bones, all flat and immobile: 4 unpaired — frontal, occipital, ethmoid and sphenoid — and 2 paired — parietal (left, right) and temporal (left, right).

There are 14 facial bones: 2 unpaired (mandible and vomer) and 6 paired (maxilla, zygomatic, nasal, inferior nasal conchae, lacrimal and palatine). They protect the sense organs of sight, smell and taste and provide a frame for muscle attachment. Note: the book says the cranium has "4 unpaired and 2 paired" bones — this means 4 unpaired bones plus 2 pairs, making 8 in total. The hyoid bone (lingual bone) gives attachment to the tongue and is unique because it does not articulate with any other bone.

Vertebral Column, Ribs and Sternum

  • The vertebral column supports body weight and maintains posture. Its regions are cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and coccygeal; the coccyx is formed by the fusion of four posterior vertebrae in the pelvic region. Between vertebrae lie intervertebral discs: an outer strong ring, the annulus fibrosus, and a soft gelatinous inner portion, the nucleus pulposus.
  • Ribs are long, twisted flat bones forming the major part of the rib cage. True ribs (7 pairs, ribs 1–7) attach directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilages; false ribs (3 pairs, ribs 8–10) attach to the cartilage of the rib above; floating ribs (2 pairs, ribs 11–12) have no anterior attachment.
  • The sternum (breast bone) lies in front of the chest, with the manubrium, body and xiphoid process.

Key Points

  • The skeleton supports and protects the body, stores 97% of body calcium and phosphorus, and makes blood cells in red marrow.
  • Total 206 bones: axial skeleton 80 bones, appendicular skeleton 126 bones.
  • Cranium: 8 bones (frontal, parietal ×2, temporal ×2, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid). Facial bones: 14, of which mandible and vomer are unpaired.
  • The hyoid does not articulate with any other bone; the coccyx is four fused vertebrae.
  • Ribs: 7 pairs true, 3 pairs false, 2 pairs floating.

mcqs.q: How many bones are there in the human skeleton in total?
mcqs.why: The human skeleton has 206 bones in total: the axial skeleton has 80 bones and the appendicular skeleton has 126 bones, and 80 + 126 = 206.

mcqs.q: What percentage of the body calcium and phosphorus does the skeleton store?
mcqs.why: One function of the skeleton listed in the notes is mineral storage: it stores 97 percent of the body calcium and phosphorus.

mcqs.q: How many bones does the cranium have?
mcqs.why: The cranium has 8 bones: 4 unpaired (frontal, occipital, ethmoid, sphenoid) plus 2 paired bones (parietal and temporal), that is 4 + 2 + 2 = 8.

mcqs.q: Which two facial bones are unpaired?
mcqs.why: Of the 14 facial bones, only 2 are unpaired, the mandible and the vomer; the other six types are paired, giving 2 + 12 = 14.

mcqs.q: The hyoid bone is unique because it:
options: Is the largest bone of the skull
Does not articulate with any other bone
Is formed by fusion of four vertebrae
mcqs.why: The hyoid or lingual bone gives attachment to the tongue and is unique because it does not articulate with any other bone.

mcqs.q: The coccyx is formed by the fusion of how many vertebrae?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the coccyx is formed by the fusion of four posterior vertebrae in the pelvic region of the vertebral column.

mcqs.q: How many pairs of true ribs are there?
mcqs.why: True ribs are 7 pairs (ribs 1 to 7) that attach directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilages; false ribs are 3 pairs and floating ribs 2 pairs.

mcqs.q: The soft gelatinous inner portion of an intervertebral disc is the:
mcqs.why: Each intervertebral disc has an outer strong ring, the annulus fibrosus, and a soft gelatinous inner portion called the nucleus pulposus.

mcqs.q: Hands and feet alone contain how many bones?
mcqs.why: Each hand has 27 bones and each foot has 26 bones, so hands and feet together contain 2 x 27 + 2 x 26 = 54 + 52 = 106 bones.

mcqs.q: Blood cells are made in red bone marrow, mostly present in:
mcqs.why: The notes state that blood cells are made in red bone marrow, which is mostly present in the ribs and limb bones.

lessons.title: Appendicular Skeleton: Girdles and Limbs
lessons.notes_html:
Compared with the axial skeleton, the appendicular skeleton is unfused. It consists of the girdles and the limbs, 126 bones in all, and it is built for movement rather than protection.

Pectoral Girdle and Fore Limb

The pectoral (shoulder) girdle connects the fore limb to the trunk. It has two bones on each side: the clavicle (collar bone, from the Latin word clavicula) and the scapula (shoulder bone, a flat triangular bone; Latin scapul means shoulder blade). The lateral depression of the scapula, the glenoid cavity, receives the head of the humerus.

There are 30 bones in each fore limb:

  • Humerus (1) — Long bone of the upper arm; its head fits into the glenoid cavity at the shoulder and its lower end forms the elbow joint with the radius and ulna.
  • Radius (1) and ulna (1) — Bones of the forearm.
  • Carpals (8) — Small bones of the wrist in two rows, giving the wrist flexibility.
  • Metacarpals (5) — Bones of the palm.
  • Phalanges (14) — Finger bones: three in each finger and two in the thumb.

Pelvic Girdle and Hind Limb

The pelvic girdle connects the hind limbs to the trunk and bears the weight of the upper body. Each hip bone is formed of ilium, ischium and pubis. Its deep socket, the acetabulum, provides the articular surface for the head of the femur.

There are 30 bones in each hind limb:

  • Femur (1) — Thigh bone, the longest bone; its head fits into the acetabulum.
  • Patella (1) — The knee cap, in front of the knee joint.
  • Tibia (1) and fibula (1) — Bones of the shank (lower leg).
  • Tarsals (7) — Larger, stronger bones of the ankle, including the calcaneus (heel bone) and talus; they bear body weight and give the foot strength and stability.
  • Metatarsals (5) and phalanges (14) — Bones of the foot and toes (three in each toe, two in the big toe).
CarpalsTarsals
8 bones of the wrist, in two rows7 bones of the ankle
Smaller, for flexibility of the wristLarger and stronger, for weight-bearing
Part of the hand (27 bones in each hand)Include calcaneus (heel) and talus; part of the foot (26 bones in each foot)

Key Points

  • The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) consists of girdles and limbs and is unfused, for movement.
  • Each fore limb has 30 bones: humerus 1, radius 1, ulna 1, carpals 8, metacarpals 5, phalanges 14.
  • Each hind limb has 30 bones: femur 1, patella 1, tibia 1, fibula 1, tarsals 7, metatarsals 5, phalanges 14.
  • The glenoid cavity of the scapula receives the humerus; the acetabulum of the hip bone receives the femur.
  • Carpals are 8 in the wrist; tarsals are 7 in the ankle.

mcqs.q: The appendicular skeleton consists of how many bones?
mcqs.why: The appendicular skeleton consists of the girdles and limbs and has 126 bones in all; the axial skeleton has the remaining 80 of the 206 total.

mcqs.q: The glenoid cavity of the scapula receives the head of the:
mcqs.why: The lateral depression of the scapula, the glenoid cavity, receives the head of the humerus, forming the shoulder joint.

mcqs.q: How many bones are there in each fore limb?
mcqs.why: Each fore limb has humerus 1 + radius 1 + ulna 1 + carpals 8 + metacarpals 5 + phalanges 14 = 30 bones in total.

mcqs.q: How many carpal bones are there in the wrist?
mcqs.why: The carpals are 8 small bones of the wrist arranged in two rows, giving the wrist flexibility, unlike the 7 stronger tarsals of the ankle.

mcqs.q: The deep socket of the hip bone that receives the head of the femur is the:
mcqs.why: Each hip bone, formed of ilium, ischium and pubis, has a deep socket called the acetabulum that provides the articular surface for the head of the femur.

mcqs.q: Which is the longest bone of the body, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The femur is the thigh bone and is described in the notes as the longest bone; its head fits into the acetabulum of the hip bone.

mcqs.q: How many phalanges are there in each hand or foot?
mcqs.why: There are 14 phalanges in each limb end: three in each finger or toe and two in the thumb or big toe, that is 4 x 3 + 2 = 14.

mcqs.q: The heel bone is called the:
mcqs.why: The tarsals include the calcaneus, which is the heel bone, and the talus; together they bear body weight and give the foot strength and stability.

mcqs.q: The clavicle is also known as the:
mcqs.why: The pectoral girdle has two bones on each side: the clavicle, called the collar bone from the Latin clavicula, and the scapula or shoulder blade.

mcqs.q: How many bones are there in each hind limb?
mcqs.why: Each hind limb has femur 1 + patella 1 + tibia 1 + fibula 1 + tarsals 7 + metatarsals 5 + phalanges 14 = 30 bones in total.

lessons.title: Joints: Fibrous, Cartilaginous and Synovial
lessons.notes_html:
A joint is the attachment (place of meeting) between two bones, or between bone and cartilage, where movement takes place. Joints are classified by the tissue connecting the bones and by how much movement they allow.

Fibrous Joints

In fibrous joints the articular surfaces are connected by dense connective tissue consisting mainly of collagen. They are immovable joints because they allow no movement. Examples: the sutures between skull bones, the joint between a tooth and its socket, and the joint between the tibia and fibula.

Cartilaginous Joints

In cartilaginous joints the bones are connected by cartilage, so they are slightly movable and allow a little movement. Examples: hyaline cartilage in the costal cartilages attaching ribs to the sternum, and fibrocartilage in the intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis.

Synovial Joints

Synovial joints are the most mobile type. The articular surfaces are covered with hyaline cartilage, a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid (secreted by the synovial membrane) lies between them, and ligaments and a joint capsule hold the joint. Synovial fluid reduces friction and lubricates the surfaces. Ball and socket, hinge and pivot joints are all synovial joints.

Type of Synovial JointExample
Ball and socket jointHip and shoulder
Hinge jointElbow and knee
Pivot jointAtlas and axis (first two neck vertebrae)
Gliding jointBetween vertebrae
Ellipsoid (condyloid) jointSkull and 1st vertebra
Saddle jointCarpometacarpal joint of the thumb

A synovial joint: articular cartilage, a fluid-filled cavity and a joint capsule.

The knee joint is the largest and most complex joint of the human body. Ligaments join bone to bone inside and around joints, while tendons join muscle to bone.

Key Points

  • A joint is where two or more bones meet; movement takes place there.
  • Fibrous joints are immovable (skull sutures, tooth socket, tibia–fibula).
  • Cartilaginous joints are slightly movable (intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, costal cartilages).
  • Synovial joints are freely movable, with synovial fluid reducing friction: hinge (elbow, knee), ball and socket (hip, shoulder), pivot (atlas–axis), gliding, ellipsoid and saddle.
  • The knee is the largest and most complex joint of the body.

mcqs.q: Fibrous joints are best described as:
options: Immovable joints joined by dense connective tissue of collagen
Freely movable joints with synovial fluid
Slightly movable joints joined by cartilage
Joints found only in the limbs
mcqs.why: In fibrous joints the articular surfaces are connected by dense connective tissue consisting mainly of collagen, so they allow no movement.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a fibrous joint?
mcqs.why: Examples of fibrous joints in the notes are the sutures between skull bones, the joint between a tooth and its socket, and the joint between tibia and fibula.

mcqs.q: Cartilaginous joints allow:
options: A little movement, being slightly movable
mcqs.why: In cartilaginous joints the bones are connected by cartilage, so they are slightly movable and allow a little movement, as in intervertebral discs.

mcqs.q: The synovial fluid in a synovial joint serves to:
options: Reduce friction and lubricate the surfaces
mcqs.why: Synovial fluid, secreted by the synovial membrane into the joint cavity, reduces friction and lubricates the articular surfaces of synovial joints.

mcqs.q: The elbow and knee are examples of which synovial joint type?
mcqs.why: The notes list the elbow and knee as hinge joints, while the hip and shoulder are ball and socket joints and atlas-axis is a pivot joint.

mcqs.q: The pivot joint in the body is found between:
mcqs.why: The pivot joint example given in the notes is the joint between the atlas and axis, the first two neck vertebrae, allowing rotation of the head.

mcqs.q: Which joint is the largest and most complex joint of the human body?

lessons.title: Disorders of the Skeleton: Disc Slip, Spondylosis, Sciatica and Arthritis
lessons.notes_html:
Deformation of the skeleton may occur due to genetic diseases, hormonal problems and nutritional deficiencies. This lesson covers the disorders of the vertebral column and joints described in section 16.2.

16.2 Disorders of Skeleton

Disc Slip (Herniated Disc)

Each intervertebral disc has an outer ring (annulus fibrosus) and a soft gelatinous centre (nucleus pulposus). In a disc slip, the nucleus pulposus bulges or leaks out through a tear in the ring and may press on a spinal nerve, causing pain. It is a common cause of back pain and of sciatica.

Spondylosis

Spondylosis is the degenerative (wear-and-tear) disease of the vertebral column, mainly of the cervical and lumbar regions, in which the discs and joints of the spine wear out with age, making the neck or back stiff and painful.

Sciatica

Sciatica refers to back pain caused by a problem with the sciatic nerve, a large nerve that travels from the lower lumbar spine to the back of each leg. Any injury to the sciatic nerve causes pain in the lower back that travels to the hip, buttocks and leg. Common causes include a herniated (slip) disc, injury to the proximal sciatic nerve, spondylolisthesis (one vertebra slipping forward over another), muscle spasm in the back or buttocks, and improper injection into the buttocks. Pregnant women have a greater chance of a herniated disc and sciatica, and diabetes can also cause nerve damage. Recovery from sciatic injury is usually slow and incomplete.

Arthritis

Arthritis is the inflammation of a joint: the joints become swollen, stiffer and painful, the membrane lining the joint thickens, and fluid production decreases, which increases friction. Possible causes are infection or injury to the joints, abnormal metabolism and immune system dysfunction, and sometimes inheritance.

  • Osteoarthritis — The most common chronic arthritis, a degenerative joint disease in which the joint cartilage degenerates (wears away); it may also be caused by inheritance.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis — Inflammation of the hand and wrist joints (including the finger joints), an immune-system disorder.
  • Gouty arthritis — Develops in people with a high level of uric acid in the blood, caused by deposition of needle-like crystals of uric acid in a joint, often the big toe.

Key Points

  • Skeletal deformities arise from genetic diseases, hormonal problems and nutritional deficiencies.
  • In disc slip the nucleus pulposus bulges out of the intervertebral disc and may press on a nerve.
  • Sciatica is pain along the sciatic nerve, from the lower back to the hip, buttock and leg; a slipped disc is a common cause.
  • Arthritis is inflammation of joints. Osteoarthritis is degenerative and most common; rheumatoid arthritis affects hand and wrist joints; gouty arthritis is due to uric acid crystals.
  • Spondylosis is age-related degeneration of the spine.

mcqs.why: Arthritis is the inflammation of a joint: the joints become swollen, stiffer and painful, the lining membrane thickens and fluid production decreases.

mcqs.why: Osteoarthritis is described as the most common chronic arthritis, a degenerative joint disease in which the joint cartilage wears away.

mcqs.why: Gouty arthritis develops in people with a high level of uric acid in the blood, from deposition of needle-like uric acid crystals, often in the big toe.

lessons.title: Fractures, Bone Healing and Joint Injuries
lessons.notes_html:
When there is a partial or complete break in the continuity of a bone, it is called a bone fracture. Fractures, dislocations and sprains are the common injuries of the skeleton, and each has its own first aid.

Types of Fractures

  • Simple (closed) fracture — The broken bones remain within the body, the skin remains intact and there is no damage to the surrounding tissues.
  • Compound (open) fracture — The broken bones penetrate the skin, or the force of injury breaks the skin, causing a risk of infection.
  • Complicated fracture — The broken bone damages the surrounding structures (organs), and there may be damage to arteries, veins and nerves; it heals more slowly.

Reduction and First Aid

Reduction is putting the broken fragments back into their normal position. In closed reduction the fragments are coaxed back by the physician's hands without surgical exposure; in open reduction surgery is performed by dissecting the tissues and the fragments are secured with pins or wires. After reduction the part is immobilized so healing can occur.

First aid for a fracture: do not move the injured part unnecessarily; immobilize it with a splint and support it in a comfortable position; apply cold to reduce swelling and pain; control any bleeding with a clean cloth and do not push back any bone that pierces the skin; keep the patient calm and still; and get medical help at once.

Healing of a Simple Fracture

Bone healing is a natural process that usually takes 8–12 weeks (longer for large weight-bearing bones, and slower in elderly people due to poor blood circulation), in four phases:

  • 1. Hematoma formation — Injured blood vessels bleed at the fracture site, the blood clots and forms a hematoma; bone cells deprived of nutrients begin to die, and the tissues swell and cause much pain.
  • 2. Soft callus formation — Within a few days capillaries grow into the hematoma and phagocytic cells clear the debris; fibroblasts produce collagen fibres connecting the ends of the broken bone while osteoblasts start forming spongy bone and some bone spicules appear. The soft callus lasts approximately 4–6 weeks.
  • 3. Hard (bony) callus formation — Osteoblasts and osteoclasts multiply rapidly, move inward and convert the soft callus into bony callus; woven bone is transformed into lamellar bone and a ring of new bone forms around the fracture, so the mended bone is slightly thicker there.
  • 4. Bone remodelling — The bony callus is remodelled by osteoblasts and osteoclasts; unwanted bits are broken down and reabsorbed, and the final mended bone is almost undetectable on X-ray. Remodelling may continue for months or even years.

Dislocation and Sprain

When the joint is moved away from its original position, it is called joint dislocation. A sprain is the stretching, tearing or twisting of ligaments. First aid for both is to rest and support the joint, apply cold to reduce swelling and pain, and seek medical help; a dislocated joint must be put back (reduced) by a trained person, not forced by untrained hands.

Key Points

  • A fracture is a partial or complete break in the continuity of a bone: simple (skin intact), compound (bone pierces skin, infection risk), complicated (organs, vessels or nerves damaged).
  • Reduction may be closed (by hand) or open (surgery with pins or wires).
  • Healing takes 8–12 weeks: hematoma, soft callus (4–6 weeks), hard callus, then remodelling.
  • Dislocation is displacement of a joint from its original position; a sprain is stretching, tearing or twisting of ligaments.
  • First aid: immobilize with a splint, apply cold, control bleeding, keep the patient still and get medical help.

lessons.title: Muscles and the Structure of Skeletal Muscle
lessons.notes_html:
The muscle is the contractile tissue found in animals, and its primary function is to produce movement. The study of muscle is called myology. A muscle is attached to bone by a connective tissue known as a tendon.

16.3 Muscles: Three Types

Skeletal MuscleCardiac MuscleSmooth Muscle
Attached to bones; striated; voluntaryOnly in the heart; striated; involuntary, controlled by the autonomic nervous systemIn walls of internal organs; non-striated; involuntary
Cells are long, cylindrical and multinucleated (polynucleated)Cells are uninucleated (single nucleus)Cells are spindle-shaped and uninucleated
Contracts quickly and strongly; fatiguesContracts rhythmically and does not fatigueContracts slowly and for long periods

Structure of Skeletal Muscle

Skeletal muscle is made of bundles (fascicles) of long, cylindrical, multinucleated muscle fibres (cells). Each fibre is covered by a membrane, the sarcolemma, whose infoldings form T-tubules, and it contains the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which stores calcium ions. Inside the fibre are myofibrils divided into sarcomeres, the structural and functional units of muscle contraction, bounded by Z-lines.

  • Each sarcomere has thin actin filaments, about 7 nm in diameter, and thick myosin filaments, about 16 nm.
  • The regular overlap of these filaments gives the striated appearance: dark bands where thick and thin filaments overlap, and light bands.
  • The end of the muscle that remains fixed when the muscle contracts is the origin; the end attached to the movable bone is the insertion; the thick middle part is the belly.

A sarcomere between two Z-lines: thin actin filaments slide over thick myosin filaments during contraction.

Key Points

  • Muscle is contractile tissue; its study is myology, and it is attached to bone by tendons.
  • Skeletal muscle is striated, voluntary and multinucleated; cardiac muscle is in the heart, involuntary and uninucleated; smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary.
  • The sarcomere, bounded by Z-lines, is the structural and functional unit of contraction.
  • Actin filaments are about 7 nm thick; myosin filaments about 16 nm. Calcium ions are required for contraction.
  • The sarcolemma's infoldings are T-tubules; the sarcoplasmic reticulum stores Ca²⁺.

lessons.title: Sliding Filament Theory, Antagonistic Movement and Muscle Disorders
lessons.notes_html:
Muscles can only pull, never push, so they are arranged in opposing pairs around joints. This lesson explains how a muscle contracts and what goes wrong in muscle disorders.

Sliding Filament Theory

The sliding filament theory explains muscle contraction. When a nerve impulse arrives, calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. They expose the binding sites on actin; the myosin heads attach to actin and, using energy from ATP, pull the thin filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere. The sarcomeres shorten, so the whole fibre — and the muscle — contracts, while the actual length of the actin and myosin filaments does not change: the actin filaments slide over the myosin filaments. When the impulse ends, calcium is pumped back and the muscle relaxes.

Antagonistic Movement

The opposite movement of flexor and extensor muscles is called antagonistic movement. Muscles work in opposing pairs: the muscle that is contracting is called the agonist, and the muscle that is relaxing is called the antagonist; for the reverse movement their roles swap. For example, at the elbow the biceps contracts to flex the arm while the triceps relaxes, and the triceps contracts to extend the arm while the biceps relaxes.

Movement of the Knee Joint

The knee joint is the largest and most complex joint of the body, a hinge-type synovial joint. The quadriceps (extensor) group on the front of the thigh contracts to extend (straighten) the knee while the hamstring (flexor) group at the back relaxes; the hamstrings contract to flex (bend) the knee while the quadriceps relax. Ligaments, the joint capsule and the patella (knee cap) stabilize the joint during this movement.

Muscle Disorders

  • Muscle fatigue — The reduced ability of a muscle to contract after prolonged or repeated activity, because ATP and glycogen are used up and lactic acid and other metabolites accumulate; the muscle feels weak and painful, and rest recovers it.
  • Cramp — A sudden, painful, involuntary contraction of a muscle or part of a muscle, usually brief, caused by overuse, dehydration or temporary electrolyte disturbance; it relaxes after a short time, often helped by stretching and rest.
  • Tetany — A disease appearing due to a low level of Ca²⁺ in the blood: the nerves become hyperexcitable and the muscles undergo sustained, involuntary contractions (spasms) that do not relax normally. Unlike a cramp, tetany is caused by a persistent low blood calcium level.

Key Points

  • In sliding filament theory, Ca²⁺ exposes actin binding sites and myosin heads pull actin to the centre; filament lengths do not change.
  • Antagonistic movement: when the agonist contracts, the antagonist relaxes, and vice versa.
  • At the knee, quadriceps extend and hamstrings flex, working antagonistically.
  • Fatigue follows prolonged activity and lactic acid accumulation; a cramp is a brief painful contraction.
  • Tetany is sustained spasm due to low Ca²⁺ in the blood.

mcqs.why: When a nerve impulse arrives, calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and expose the binding sites on actin for the myosin heads.

mcqs.why: The lesson begins by stating that muscles can only pull, never push, so they are arranged in opposing antagonistic pairs around joints.

lessons.title: Nervous Coordination, Receptors and Effectors
lessons.notes_html:
All animals respond to stimuli, that is, any internal or external change. The activities of different body parts in response to stimuli must be coordinated, and this coordination makes the integration of functions essential to animal behaviour possible. In humans and most animals there are two types of coordination: nervous coordination and endocrine coordination. This unit deals only with nervous coordination.

17.1 Nervous System of Man

The study of the nervous system is known as neurology. The working of different body parts in cooperation with each other and under the control of a coordinator (brain, spinal cord or ganglia) is called coordination. The system of the body that provides coordination through electric signals among different body parts during the response to a particular stimulus is called the nervous system. The most developed, advanced and evolved nervous system among all organisms is that of humans.

17.1.1 Steps Involved in Nervous Coordination

Nervous coordination involves highly specialized cells known as neurons, which are either connected together or linked via the centralized nervous system to form a network that is linked to the receptors and effectors. The nervous system in humans and higher animals consists of three basic elements:

  • Receptors — Cells, tissues or organs which receive stimuli and give information to sensory neurons.
  • The neuron — It has the capacity to generate and conduct impulses to the central nervous system, where processing and analysis of information takes place, and to pass responses to the effectors.
  • Effectors — Structures such as cells, tissues, muscles and glands which carry out action or make responses.

17.1.2 Receptors or Transducers

Receptors are organs, tissues, cells or nerve endings that detect changes (stimuli) in the external or internal environment of an animal. These stimuli are then transmitted to the brain or spinal cord through sensory neurons. Receptors act as transducers because they convert the energy of the stimulus into nerve impulses.

On the basis of stimuli, receptors are classified into five types:

  • Chemoreceptors — Detect the concentration of certain chemicals or ions, e.g. CO₂ level in the blood by the medulla of the brain and O₂ level by the carotid body. Chemoreceptors for blood glucose, amino acids and fatty acids are located in the hypothalamus of the brain; smell (olfaction) is in the nasal epithelium, taste (gustation) is found in the tongue, and osmoreceptors (which detect osmotic pressure of blood) are in the hypothalamus.
  • Mechanoreceptors — Detect stimuli of pressure, body position or acceleration. They include Meissner's corpuscles in the skin for touch, Pacinian's corpuscles also in the skin, baroreceptors in blood vessels for pressure, and stretch receptors in the ear for hearing and equilibrium.
  • Thermoreceptors — Mostly located in the skin to detect changes in temperature (cold and warmth).
  • Nociceptors — Pain receptors, widely distributed in the skin and other internal organs, which detect damage to body tissues.
  • Photoreceptors or electromagnetic receptors — Detect light stimuli, such as rods and cone cells in the retina of our eyes.

17.1.3 Processing / Analysis of Information

All types of sensory inputs from various receptors are conveyed to the coordinator, i.e. the brain and spinal cord, by sensory neurons. The information collected by them is processed and analysed for a suitable response by special types of neurons known as inter neurons, also called associated or relay neurons.

17.1.4 Effectors

Effectors respond to stimuli by impulses coming via motor neurons, such as muscles and glands. The glands secrete some types of chemicals, while muscles respond by contracting. The whole pathway can be summarized as: Stimulus → Receptor → Sensory neuron → Inter neuron (CNS) → Motor neuron → Effector → Response.

Key Points

  • Coordination is of two types: nervous coordination (by electric signals) and endocrine coordination; the study of the nervous system is neurology.
  • The three basic elements of nervous coordination are receptors, neurons (with the CNS as coordinator) and effectors.
  • Receptors are transducers: chemoreceptors, mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors, nociceptors and photoreceptors.
  • Meissner's corpuscles detect touch, Pacinian's corpuscles detect pressure, and nociceptors detect pain.
  • Inter (associated or relay) neurons in the CNS process and analyse information; muscles and glands are the principal effectors.

mcqs.why: Nociceptors are pain receptors, widely distributed in the skin and other internal organs, which detect damage to body tissues.

mcqs.why: The notes state that chemoreceptors for blood glucose, amino acids and fatty acids are located in the hypothalamus, which also contains the osmoreceptors.

lessons.title: Structure of a Neuron
lessons.notes_html:
Neurons are the chief structural and functional units of the nervous system. In addition to neurons, the nervous system contains neuroglial cells, which nourish the neurons and also protect them by the myelin sheath. The nervous system also contains about 50% neuroglial cells.

17.2 Neurons

A neuron generates and conducts nerve impulses. Its structure is specialized for receiving stimuli, conducting impulses and passing them on to the next neuron, muscle or gland.

17.2.1 Structure of Neuron

A typical neuron consists of three basic components, i.e. cell body, axon and dendrites.

  • Cell body — Also called soma, cyton or perikaryon. It contains the nucleus and various cellular organelles except centrioles. The neuron cell body contains a mass of granular cytoplasm enclosed by the cell membrane, and the nucleus is centrally placed. The cell body contains a group of ribosomes associated with rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi bodies known as Nissl's granules, which help in protein synthesis and in forming the acetylcholine-forming enzyme. These granules are absent in the axon and dendron.
  • Axon — A cytoplasmic process that conducts impulses away from the cell body. Each axon is a usually thick, long fibre (a few millimetres to more than a metre in length) with a constant diameter. The cytoplasm of the axon is called axoplasm and its cell membrane is called axolemma. Each axon terminates by branching to form small extensions with knob-like endings called presynaptic terminals. The fibres at the end of the axon are its terminal branches (telodendria).
  • Dendrites — Cytoplasmic extensions that carry impulses towards the cell body. If single, the fibre is called a dendron. They are thin, short and mostly branched, and the branches are gradually tapered from the base to their tips. The gap between the dendrites of one neuron and the axon terminals of another neuron is called a synapse.

The cell body of a neuron is surrounded by cytoplasmic fibres, which are of two main types, i.e. axon and dendrites. The neuroglia or glial cells nourish, protect and support the neurons. In the peripheral nervous system these cells are known as Schwann cells, which cover the axon by repeatedly wrapping around it. These cells are also covered by a fatty substance known as the myelin sheath, which acts as an insulator, so such axons are called myelinated fibres. The non-myelinated portion of the axon between two Schwann cells is called a node of Ranvier. The impulses jump from node of Ranvier to node of Ranvier, which is known as saltatory conduction. The outer Schwann-cell membrane covering the nerve fibre is the neurilemma.

Note: On page 97 the book loosely calls the cell-body membrane the neurilemma. Strictly, as the book's own exercise answer confirms, the neurilemma is the outer membrane of the Schwann cell covering the nerve fibre (axon).

A typical neuron: dendrites carry impulses to the cell body, and the myelinated axon carries them away to the axon terminals.

Key Points

  • A neuron has three parts: cell body (soma or cyton), dendrites and axon.
  • Nissl's granules are groups of ribosomes with rough ER and Golgi bodies in the cell body; they help in protein synthesis and are absent in the axon and dendron.
  • Dendrites conduct impulses towards the cell body; the axon conducts them away from the cell body.
  • Axoplasm is the axon cytoplasm and axolemma is its membrane; the axon ends in telodendria with synaptic knobs.
  • Schwann cells form the insulating myelin sheath; the gaps between them are nodes of Ranvier, across which impulses jump in saltatory conduction.

options: Rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi bodies
mcqs.why: Nissl granules are a group of ribosomes associated with rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi bodies, helping protein synthesis; they are absent in axon and dendron.

mcqs.why: The notes state that the cell body (soma, cyton or perikaryon) contains the nucleus and various cellular organelles except centrioles.

mcqs.why: Dendrites are thin, short, branched cytoplasmic extensions that carry impulses towards the cell body, while the axon conducts impulses away from it.

mcqs.why: The notes name the cytoplasm of the axon axoplasm and its cell membrane axolemma; the axon may be a few millimetres to more than a metre long.

mcqs.why: Each axon terminates by branching, and the fibres at the end of the axon are its terminal branches called telodendria, ending in presynaptic terminals.

mcqs.why: In the PNS the neuroglial cells are Schwann cells, which cover the axon by repeatedly wrapping around it and form the fatty myelin sheath.

mcqs.why: The non-myelinated portion of the axon between two Schwann cells is called a node of Ranvier, and impulses jump between these nodes.

options: Move slowly through the cell body

lessons.title: Types of Neurons and the Reflex Arc
lessons.notes_html:
On the basis of function, neurons are of three types: sensory neurons, inter neurons and motor neurons. Together they form the pathway of every nervous response, best seen in the reflex arc.

17.2.2 Types of Neurons

  • Sensory neurons — Conduct impulses from receptors to the central nervous system. These are unipolar, because only one fibre originates from the cell body, which immediately gives rise to two branches, one towards the receptor and the other towards the central nervous system. Both fibres are structurally axon-like, except that their terminal portions differ: one behaves like dendrites and the other like an axon. The majority of sensory neurons are unipolar, but some are bipolar. The unipolar neurons are found especially in the dorsal root of the spinal cord, and their cell bodies lie outside the CNS, e.g. in dorsal root ganglia.
  • Associated or interneurons — Found only in the brain and spinal cord. They conduct impulses from sensory neurons to motor neurons and also convey messages between various parts of the CNS. Interneurons are mostly multipolar, because many fibres arise from the cell body. Their axon is thin and non-myelinated, while many dendrites carry impulses to the cell body.
  • Motor neurons — Conduct impulses from the CNS to effectors. These are multipolar neurons. Their cell body, which lies inside the CNS, contains many branched dendrites, and a single long axon runs towards the effector.

By structure, neurons are also described as multipolar (many fibres from the cell body), bipolar (two fibres) and unipolar (one fibre), as shown in the book's Fig. 17.2.

Myelinated and Non-Myelinated Neurons

Myelinated neurons (nerve fibres) are covered by a fatty layer known as the myelin sheath around the axon, whereas non-myelinated neurons do not have a myelin sheath (dendrites and cell bodies are non-myelinated). In myelinated neurons, conduction of impulses is faster than in non-myelinated neurons: the nerve impulse is 20 times faster in a myelinated neuron than in a non-myelinated neuron, because the impulse jumps from node of Ranvier to node of Ranvier (saltatory impulse). Interneurons are non-myelinated, while motor and sensory neurons have myelinated portions. Myelinated fibres have larger and thicker axons, because the velocity of the impulse depends upon the diameter, length and myelin sheath.

Sensory NeuronMotor Neuron
Carries impulses from receptors to the CNSCarries impulses from the CNS to effectors
Cell body lies outside the CNS (e.g. dorsal root ganglion)Cell body lies inside the CNS
Usually unipolarMultipolar
Dendron connected to a receptorAxon ends at a muscle or gland

17.2.3 Reflex Action and Reflex Arc

Reflex actions or reflexes are involuntary, automatic, unconscious or immediate responses to external or internal environmental changes or stimuli. The pathway through which a reflex travels is called the reflex arc. The direction of a reflex action is from receptor to sensory neuron to CNS to inter neuron and then through the motor neuron to the effectors. Reflexes have no involvement of the conscious portion of the brain, therefore the response is quicker than the conscious pathway.

Example: If we unexpectedly touch a hot object or get a pin prick, our hand is rapidly removed from it. The receptors of the hand are activated by the heat of the object. This impulse is conveyed by the sensory neuron, leading to the spinal cord via the spinal nerve, then to the inter neuron, which lies entirely within the spinal cord. The inter neuron then passes this impulse to the motor neuron and then to the effectors, i.e. muscles, which causes them to contract.

The five fundamental parts of a reflex arc are: (1) receptor, (2) sensory neuron, (3) centre (inter neuron in the brain or spinal cord), (4) motor neuron and (5) effector. A reflex action is the response itself, while the reflex arc is the route the impulse travels.

The five parts of a reflex arc, in the order the impulse travels.

Key Points

  • Sensory neurons (mostly unipolar) carry impulses from receptors to the CNS; motor neurons (multipolar) carry them from the CNS to effectors; interneurons (multipolar) link the two inside the CNS.
  • Impulse conduction is about 20 times faster in myelinated than in non-myelinated neurons, by saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.
  • A reflex action is an immediate, involuntary and automatic response; the reflex arc is its pathway.
  • The five parts of a reflex arc are receptor, sensory neuron, centre, motor neuron and effector.
  • Reflexes do not involve the conscious part of the brain, so they are quicker than conscious responses and protect the body.

mcqs.why: The majority of sensory neurons are unipolar, because only one fibre originates from the cell body and immediately gives rise to two branches.

options: Outside the CNS, e.g. in dorsal root ganglia
mcqs.why: Unipolar sensory neurons are found especially in the dorsal root of the spinal cord, and their cell bodies lie outside the CNS in dorsal root ganglia.

mcqs.why: Associated or interneurons are found only in the brain and spinal cord, where they conduct impulses from sensory neurons to motor neurons.

mcqs.why: The notes state that the nerve impulse is 20 times faster in a myelinated neuron than in a non-myelinated neuron because of saltatory conduction.

options: An involuntary, automatic, immediate response to a stimulus
A response planned by the cerebrum
mcqs.why: Reflex actions are involuntary, automatic, unconscious or immediate responses to environmental changes, with no involvement of the conscious portion of the brain.

mcqs.q: How many fundamental parts does a reflex arc have?
mcqs.why: The five fundamental parts of a reflex arc are receptor, sensory neuron, centre (inter neuron), motor neuron and effector, in that order.

mcqs.q: Motor neurons are structurally:
options: Multipolar, with the cell body inside the CNS
Bipolar, with the cell body in ganglia
mcqs.why: Motor neurons are multipolar neurons whose cell body lies inside the CNS, with many branched dendrites and a single long axon to the effector.

mcqs.why: In the example, the impulse reaches the spinal cord via the spinal nerve, then the inter neuron, which lies entirely within the spinal cord, passes it to the motor neuron.

mcqs.q: The difference between a reflex action and a reflex arc is that the arc is:
options: The pathway or route the impulse travels
mcqs.why: The notes distinguish them: a reflex action is the response itself, while the reflex arc is the route the impulse travels to produce that response.

mcqs.why: Interneurons are mostly multipolar and non-myelinated with a thin axon, while motor and sensory neurons have myelinated portions.

lessons.title: The Nerve Impulse and Resting Membrane Potential
lessons.notes_html:
A nerve impulse is the information about a stimulus that is transmitted from receptors to the CNS and from the CNS to the effectors. It is a wave of electrochemical change which runs along the length of the neuron, involving chemical reactions and movement of ions across the neurilemma.

17.3 Nerve Impulse

The measurement of the capacity to do electrical work is known as electric potential. It represents a type of stored energy produced during the separation of charge through a barrier; the charges are positive or negative, and the plasma membrane of the neuron acts as the separating barrier. An oscilloscope is an instrument with a screen which displays changes in the voltage on both sides of the plasma membrane of a neuron with time. The electric potential which exists across a cell membrane is known as membrane potential, which is either the resting membrane potential (RMP) or the action membrane potential (AMP). In humans, the normal speed of flow of impulse in a neuron is about 100–120 m/second. The refractory period lasts for about four milliseconds, so a neuron can conduct 250 impulses per second.

17.3.1 Resting Membrane Potential

A typical neuron at rest, or a non-conducting neuron, is said to be in the resting membrane potential state. In this case the neuron is more positive electrically outside than inside the plasma membrane, while the inside is more negative as compared to the outside. It measures about −70 millivolts (−0.07 volt). The non-conducting neuron is in a polarized state, and the RMP is maintained in an undisturbed membrane. If it is disturbed or stimulated by a sufficient stimulus, known as the threshold, then an action potential will occur.

Factors Involved in Resting Membrane Potential (RMP)

Sodium and potassium ions: Many kinds of ions are present inside and outside the plasma membrane of neurons, but the most important are sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺) ions. Sodium ions are tenfold higher in concentration outside than inside the membrane, whereas potassium ions are thirty fold higher in concentration inside than outside the membrane. The membranes of all nerve cells possess sodium and potassium pumps, which transport these ions with the help of energy (ATP) against their concentration gradients: for every two potassium ions actively transported inside the membrane, three sodium ions are pumped out. Thus the inside becomes more negative (−70 mV) than the outside of the plasma membrane.

IonInside (mmol/L)Outside (mmol/L)
Sodium ions15145
Potassium ions1505
Negative ions15630

Table 17.1: Ionic concentration inside and outside a resting neuron.

Negative organic ions: Many types of large negative organic compounds are present on both sides of the plasma membrane of neurons. These organic ions include some proteins, amino acids, RNA, SO₄ and PO₄. These negative ions are much more concentrated inside the membrane than outside (outside, Cl⁻ ions are present), where they are only in negligible concentration. Thus the inside is more negative than the outside.

Channel proteins (gates): The plasma membrane is virtually impermeable to all ions except potassium ions. It is slightly permeable to potassium, so K⁺ leaks out of the neuron by diffusion. That is why the inside becomes more negative than the outside of the plasma membrane of the neuron.

Key Points

  • A nerve impulse is a wave of electrochemical change along the neuron; in humans it travels at about 100–120 m/second.
  • The resting membrane potential is about −70 mV (−0.07 volt), inside negative and outside positive: the polarized state.
  • Na⁺ is tenfold higher outside and K⁺ is thirty fold higher inside the resting neuron.
  • The sodium–potassium pump uses ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ pumped in.
  • Large negative organic ions trapped inside, and leakage of K⁺ out through channel proteins, keep the inside negative.
  • The refractory period is about 4 milliseconds, so a neuron can conduct about 250 impulses per second.

options: Inside than outside the membrane (145 inside, 15 outside)
