mcqs.why: Gonorrhoea is caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae; in the male typical symptoms are pain upon urination and a thick greenish yellow urethral discharge.

mcqs.q: What serious effect can gonorrhoea have on a baby exposed during birth?
options: Heart damage in the baby only
An eye infection leading to blindness
mcqs.why: If a baby is exposed to gonorrhoea during birth, an eye infection leading to blindness can result; in adults it can also spread internally causing heart damage or arthritis.

mcqs.q: How is gonorrhoea treated, and is there a blood test for it?
options: There is no treatment; a blood test diagnoses it
Treated with penicillin or tetracycline; there is no blood test to diagnose it
Treated only by surgery; diagnosed by urine hCG test
It has no cure like AIDS
mcqs.why: The notes state there is no blood test to diagnose gonorrhoea, and it is treated using the antibiotics penicillin or tetracycline.

mcqs.q: What are the three stages of syphilis?
options: Primary: discharge; Secondary: chancre; Tertiary: rash
Primary: hard chancre; Secondary: rash all over the body; Tertiary: damage to cardiovascular and nervous systems
Only one stage with a hard chancre
mcqs.why: Syphilis has three stages separated by latent periods: primary hard chancre, secondary rash all over the body, and tertiary effects on cardiovascular and nervous systems.

mcqs.q: Syphilis is caused by which organism?
mcqs.why: Syphilis is caused by a spirochete bacterium, Treponema pallidum, and sexual contact is the major source of its dissemination.

mcqs.q: How does HIV destroy the body immune system?
options: It attacks a specific type of white blood cells called T-cells
It damages the heart and joints
mcqs.why: AIDS is caused by HIV, the Human Immunodeficiency Virus, which destroys the immune system by attacking a specific type of white blood cells called T-cells.

mcqs.q: At the end of 2019, about 38 million people were living with HIV, of whom 26 million were in the African region. What percentage lived in the African region?
mcqs.why: Working: 26 divided by 38 multiplied by 100 = 0.6842 x 100 = 68.42 percent, about 68 percent, which matches the notes saying over two thirds live in the African region.

mcqs.q: Which statement about AIDS is correct according to the notes?
options: AIDS can be cured with penicillin
HIV is transmitted only by blood transfusion
Rapid diagnostic tests can cure HIV
HIV is transmitted most prominently through sexual transmission, also via blood transfusion and contaminated syringes; still there is no cure for AIDS
mcqs.why: HIV may transmit through blood transfusion, contaminated syringes and surgical instruments, but the most prominent cause is sexual transmission, and there is still no cure for AIDS.

mcqs.q: Which measure helps prevent HIV transmission?
options: Using unsterilized needles for ear piercing
Screening donor blood before transfusion and using disposable syringes and sterilized operation tools
mcqs.why: Prevention measures include screening donor blood before transfusion, using disposable syringes and sterilized tools, avoiding blood-contaminated instruments, and affected mothers avoiding breastfeeding.

lessons.title: Embryonic Development: Cleavage and Cleavage Patterns
lessons.notes_html:
What happens before birth is even more crucial than what happens after it: if an infant does not develop properly before birth, normal growth after birth becomes difficult and sometimes impossible. The embryo is the early stage of the young one up to the formation of organs, and the study of development from fertilized egg to formation of all major organs is called embryology.

21.1 Embryonic Development

Development begins with the formation of gametes (eggs and sperms) inside the reproductive organs of the parents. Fertilization, the second stage, starts when the plasma membrane of the sperm fuses with the plasma membrane of an egg and ends when the egg nucleus and sperm nucleus fuse, forming a zygote. After zygote formation, embryonic development has four stages: (i) cleavage, (ii) gastrulation, (iii) organogenesis and (iv) growth.

21.1.1 Cleavage

Cleavage is a programme of mitotic cell division that divides the volume of the zygote cytoplasm into a number of smaller, nucleated cells called blastomeres. In cleavage the number of cells increases but the size of the cells hardly increases, so the whole embryo stays about the same size as the zygote.

  • Morulation — After many cleavages the zygote is transformed into a solid, compact, mulberry-like ball of cells known as the morula (day 4 in humans).
  • Blastulation — Cleavage continues and the cells arrange themselves to form the blastula, a hollow ball of cells containing a fluid-filled cavity, the blastocoel. In mammals this stage is called the blastocyst: a hollow sphere of large, flattened cells, the trophoblast, with 20–30 small rounded cells, the inner cell mass, at one side (day 5).

21.1.2 Different Patterns of Cleavage Based on the Amount of Yolk

Yolk is a mixture of proteins, fats, phospholipids, calcium and some other minerals, and serves as food for the developing embryo. Eggs of most invertebrates and simple chordates are isolecithal: small amounts of yolk uniformly distributed. Eggs of higher chordates such as birds and reptiles are telolecithal: a large amount of yolk concentrated at one side, the vegetal pole; the opposite pole, where the embryo is placed, is the animal pole.

  • Holoblastic cleavage — The entire egg divides into daughter cells, e.g. in isolecithal eggs of bony fish and amphibians, and in mammals.
  • Meroblastic cleavage — Cell division occurs only in the blastodisc (the small disc of cytoplasm at the animal pole), e.g. eggs of reptiles, birds and some fish; also called discoidal or partial cleavage.
  • Radial cleavage occurs in most deuterostomes, the plane of division parallel to the vertical axis; spiral cleavage occurs in most protostomes, the divisions diagonal to the vertical axis. Some ecdysozoans (arthropods, nematodes) show radial or superficial (insects) cleavage, and tunicates and mammals have specialized patterns.

Key Points

  • Embryology is the study of development from fertilized egg to organ formation; stages after the zygote are cleavage, gastrulation, organogenesis and growth.
  • Cleavage produces blastomeres; cell number increases but cell size hardly increases, so the morula is the same size as the zygote.
  • The morula is a solid ball; the blastula (blastocyst in mammals) is a hollow ball with a blastocoel, trophoblast and inner cell mass.
  • Holoblastic cleavage divides the whole egg; meroblastic cleavage divides only the blastodisc of yolky (telolecithal) eggs.
  • Radial cleavage is found in deuterostomes; spiral cleavage in protostomes.

mcqs.q: What is embryology?
options: The study of development from fertilized egg to formation of all major organs
The study of gamete production only
mcqs.why: Embryology is defined as the study of development from the fertilized egg to the formation of all major organs; the embryo is the early stage up to organ formation.

mcqs.q: What is the correct sequence of stages after zygote formation in embryonic development?
mcqs.why: After zygote formation, embryonic development has four stages in order: cleavage, gastrulation, organogenesis and growth, as listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: What happens during cleavage?
options: Cells grow much larger and the embryo doubles in size
Mitotic division divides the zygote cytoplasm into smaller nucleated blastomeres; cell number increases but cell size hardly increases, so the embryo stays about the same size as the zygote
Cells arrange into three germ layers
Organs and organ systems are formed
mcqs.why: Cleavage is a programme of mitotic division producing blastomeres; number increases but size hardly increases, so the whole embryo stays about the same size as the zygote.

mcqs.q: What is the morula, and when does it form in humans?
options: A hollow ball with a blastocoel; day 5
A solid, compact, mulberry-like ball of cells; day 4 in humans
mcqs.why: After many cleavages the zygote becomes a solid compact mulberry-like ball of cells called the morula, which in humans is the day 4 stage.

mcqs.q: What is the mammalian blastocyst made of?
options: A hollow sphere of large flattened trophoblast cells with 20-30 small rounded inner cell mass cells at one side
Only a solid mass of blastomeres
Three germ layers around an archenteron
mcqs.why: In mammals the blastula stage is the blastocyst (day 5): a hollow sphere of trophoblast with 20 to 30 small rounded inner cell mass cells at one side, around the blastocoel.

mcqs.q: What is yolk, and what is its function?
options: A fluid that fills the blastocoel only
A membrane surrounding the mammalian ovum
A mixture of proteins, fats, phospholipids, calcium and some other minerals that serves as food for the developing embryo
mcqs.why: Yolk is described as a mixture of proteins, fats, phospholipids, calcium and other minerals, and it serves as food for the developing embryo.

mcqs.q: What are telolecithal eggs?
options: Eggs with small amounts of yolk uniformly distributed
Eggs with no yolk at all
Eggs of birds and reptiles with a large amount of yolk concentrated at one side, the vegetal pole
Eggs that divide only at the blastodisc surface
mcqs.why: Eggs of higher chordates such as birds and reptiles are telolecithal: a large amount of yolk concentrated at the vegetal pole, with the embryo at the opposite animal pole.

mcqs.q: What is holoblastic cleavage?
options: Division occurs only in the blastodisc
The entire egg divides into daughter cells, as in isolecithal eggs of bony fish and amphibians and in mammals
Division diagonal to the vertical axis in protostomes
Division parallel to the vertical axis in deuterostomes
mcqs.why: In holoblastic cleavage the entire egg divides into daughter cells, for example in isolecithal eggs of bony fish and amphibians and in mammals.

mcqs.q: What is meroblastic (discoidal) cleavage, and in which eggs does it occur?
options: The whole egg divides; in mammal eggs
Cells divide spirally; in protostome eggs
No division occurs; in isolecithal eggs
Cell division occurs only in the blastodisc at the animal pole; in eggs of reptiles, birds and some fish
mcqs.why: Meroblastic cleavage, also called discoidal or partial cleavage, occurs only in the blastodisc, the small disc of cytoplasm at the animal pole, in eggs of reptiles, birds and some fish.

mcqs.q: How do radial and spiral cleavage differ in occurrence?
options: Radial occurs in most deuterostomes with divisions parallel to the vertical axis; spiral occurs in most protostomes with divisions diagonal to the vertical axis
Radial occurs in protostomes; spiral in deuterostomes
mcqs.why: Radial cleavage occurs in most deuterostomes, the plane of division parallel to the vertical axis, while spiral cleavage occurs in most protostomes, divisions diagonal to the vertical axis.

lessons.title: Gastrulation and the Three Germ Layers
lessons.notes_html:
Gastrulation is the stage of major cellular reorganization in which the newly formed cells become arranged into two or three primary tissue layers, the germ layers, whose descendants will form all the tissues and organs of the adult.

21.1.3 Gastrulation

  • Ectoderm (outer layer) — The outermost layer, the one that forms first. It forms the integument (outer layer of skin, hair, nails, feathers and scales), the nervous system and parts of sense organs, and the inner layer of mouth, rectum, anus and teeth.
  • Mesoderm (middle layer) — It gives rise to the skeleton, muscles, blood and blood vessels, reproductive organs, connective tissues, excretory organs, lymphatic tissue and the innermost layer of the skin. The formation of mesoderm was a pivotal step in the evolution of nearly all large complex animals.
  • Endoderm (inner layer) — The innermost layer. It gives rise to the lining of the digestive tract, digestive organs and associated glands, the respiratory tract, lungs, urinary bladder and urethra.

In two-layered animals such as coelenterates, instead of mesoderm a jelly-like mesogloea is present between ectoderm and endoderm; it functions as a hydrostatic skeleton.

The gastrula: ectoderm outside, mesoderm in the middle and endoderm inside; every organ forms from these three layers.

Gastrulation in Human

In the human embryo gastrulation begins during the 3rd week of pregnancy. The trophoblast thickens at one point to form the inner cell mass, which after implantation breaks into two fluid-filled sacs separated by a double layer of cells, the embryonic disc. One sac is the amniotic sac (amnion), filled with amniotic fluid; the other is the yolk sac, which in humans contains no yolk because the embryo gets nutrients from the mother, first from the uterus lining and later by the placenta.

Gastrulation begins when a groove with raised edges, the primitive streak, appears on the dorsal surface of the embryonic disc and establishes the longitudinal axis of the embryo. At its cephalic end, closely packed cells from a local thickening form Hensen's node (printed "Hansen's node" in the exercise). The surface cells, the epiblast (upper layer), migrate and enter the primitive streak. The lower layer is the hypoblast, which is the future (presumptive) endoderm; the epiblast gives rise to ectoderm, and ectoderm cells migrating through the streak into the interior form the mesoderm. The cavity formed between the somatic and splanchnic layers of mesoderm is the coelom, and the primitive gut inside is the archenteron.

Key Points

  • Gastrulation arranges cells into ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm; all adult tissues and organs come from these layers.
  • Ectoderm forms skin covering, nervous system and sense organs; mesoderm forms skeleton, muscles, blood, kidneys and gonads; endoderm lines the gut and respiratory tract and forms their glands.
  • In humans gastrulation starts in the 3rd week at the primitive streak, with Hensen's node at its cephalic end.
  • The epiblast is the upper layer of the blastoderm and the hypoblast the lower layer, mainly presumptive endoderm.
  • The blastocyst has an inner cell mass that forms the embryo and a trophoblast that gives rise to the placenta.

mcqs.q: What does the ectoderm form?
options: Lining of the digestive tract and lungs
Integument (skin covering, hair, nails), nervous system and parts of sense organs
mcqs.why: The ectoderm is the outermost layer forming first; it forms the integument, nervous system, parts of sense organs and inner layer of mouth, rectum, anus and teeth.

mcqs.q: Which structures arise from the mesoderm?
options: Skeleton, muscles, blood and blood vessels, reproductive and excretory organs and connective tissues
Lining of the gut and respiratory tract
mcqs.why: The mesoderm, the middle layer, gives rise to skeleton, muscles, blood and vessels, reproductive organs, connective tissues, excretory organs and lymphatic tissue.

mcqs.q: What does the endoderm give rise to?
options: Lining of the digestive tract, digestive organs and glands, respiratory tract, lungs, urinary bladder and urethra
mcqs.why: The endoderm is the innermost layer giving rise to the lining of the digestive tract, digestive organs and associated glands, respiratory tract, lungs, bladder and urethra.

mcqs.q: In two-layered animals such as coelenterates, what is present instead of mesoderm?
options: A jelly-like mesogloea between ectoderm and endoderm, functioning as a hydrostatic skeleton
mcqs.why: In coelenterates, instead of mesoderm a jelly-like mesogloea is present between ectoderm and endoderm and functions as a hydrostatic skeleton.

mcqs.q: When does gastrulation begin in the human embryo, and where does it start?
options: During the 1st week, at the neural plate
During the 4th week, at the notochord
During the 3rd month, in the placenta
During the 3rd week, when the primitive streak appears on the dorsal surface of the embryonic disc
mcqs.why: In the human embryo gastrulation begins during the 3rd week of pregnancy, starting when the primitive streak appears on the dorsal surface of the embryonic disc.

mcqs.q: What is Hensen's node?
options: A local thickening of closely packed cells at the cephalic end of the primitive streak
A fluid-filled sac beside the embryonic disc
The primitive gut inside the gastrula
mcqs.why: At the cephalic end of the primitive streak, closely packed cells form a local thickening called Hensen's node, as described in the gastrulation notes.

mcqs.q: What are the epiblast and hypoblast?
options: Epiblast is the lower layer; hypoblast is the upper layer
Epiblast is the upper layer giving rise to ectoderm; hypoblast is the lower layer, the future presumptive endoderm
Both are parts of the trophoblast only
mcqs.why: The epiblast is the upper surface layer that gives rise to ectoderm, while the lower hypoblast is the future presumptive endoderm; migrating cells through the streak form mesoderm.

mcqs.q: Why does the human yolk sac contain no yolk?
options: Because the yolk is used up during cleavage
Because the embryo gets nutrients from the mother, first from the uterus lining and later by the placenta
Because the amnion absorbs all the yolk
mcqs.why: The human yolk sac contains no yolk because the embryo gets nutrients from the mother, first from the uterus lining and later by the placenta.

mcqs.q: What are the coelom and the archenteron?
options: Coelom is the cavity formed between somatic and splanchnic layers of mesoderm; archenteron is the primitive gut inside
Coelom is the primitive gut; archenteron is the body cavity
Both are fluid-filled sacs of the blastocyst
Both are parts of the neural tube
mcqs.why: The cavity formed between the somatic and splanchnic layers of mesoderm is the coelom, and the primitive gut inside the gastrula is the archenteron.

mcqs.q: What does the primitive streak establish in the embryo?
options: The transverse axis of the embryo
The position of the placenta only
The longitudinal axis of the embryo
mcqs.why: The primitive streak, a groove with raised edges on the dorsal surface of the embryonic disc, establishes the longitudinal axis of the embryo.

lessons.title: Neurulation, Neural Crest, Organogenesis and Growth
lessons.notes_html:
After gastrulation, the first major phase of organ formation is the building of the nervous system. The embryo at this stage is called the neurula.

21.1.4 Neurilation in Human Embryo

Neurulation begins during the fourth week of pregnancy. The mesodermal cells immediately beneath the early primitive streak aggregate to form a rod of mesodermal cells called the notochord, the first axial support of the embryo. The notochordal cells induce the overlying ectoderm to thicken, forming the neural plate. The central region of the neural plate pushes downward to form a depression, the neural groove, then the neural fold. The cells in the neural fold move to the upper margin and ultimately fuse to form the neural tube, which pinches off and becomes covered by surface ectoderm. At this point the embryo is designated as neurula.

The neural tube grows and differentiates into the brain and spinal cord. At the end of the fourth week the vesicles of fore, mid and hind brain are formed, while at the end of the eighth to ninth week all flexures are evident. Failure of the protective covering to close around the spinal cord leaves a gap and causes spina bifida, which can lead to permanent nerve damage and sometimes paralysis.

21.1.5 The Formation of Neural Crest and Its Derivatives

Many motor nerves arise from the developing brain and spinal cord, but the sensory nerves have a separate origin, the neural crest, developed in the region of the neural plate border. Neural crest cells migrate widely to the lateral side of the neural tube and give rise to the nerves and sympathetic ganglia. They also help in the formation of the cortical region of medulla, skull bone, teeth and many other parts. Therefore many embryologists consider the neural crest as the fourth germ layer.

21.1.6 Organogenesis

Organogenesis is the stage of development in which the formation of organs and organ systems takes place during embryonic development. The first major step in organogenesis is neurulation, the differentiation of ectoderm that produces the brain and spinal cord; all other organs then develop from the three germ layers.

21.1.7 Growth

Growth is the last step of development. It begins by the start of the third month (in the human embryo) and ends long after birth, and is characterized by increase in size and mass of the organism. From the third month till birth the human embryo is called the fetus, and the rest of the developmental period comprises only growth and maturation of organs and organ systems.

Key Points

  • Neurulation (4th week): notochord induces ectoderm to form neural plate, groove and folds, which fuse into the neural tube.
  • The neural tube becomes the brain and spinal cord; the embryo at this stage is the neurula.
  • Neural crest cells, from the neural plate border, form sensory nerves, sympathetic ganglia, parts of skull and teeth, and are called the fourth germ layer.
  • Organogenesis is the formation of organs and organ systems; neurulation is its first major step.
  • Growth begins at the start of the third month; from then until birth the embryo is called a fetus.

mcqs.q: When does neurulation begin, and what is the notochord?
options: In the 3rd week; a fluid-filled sac
In the 3rd month; a part of the placenta
During the fourth week; a rod of mesodermal cells beneath the primitive streak forming the first axial support
At birth; a part of the spinal cord only
mcqs.why: Neurulation begins during the fourth week; mesodermal cells beneath the early primitive streak aggregate to form the notochord, a rod that is the first axial support of the embryo.

mcqs.q: What is the correct sequence in neural tube formation?
options: Notochord induces ectoderm to form neural plate, then neural groove, then neural fold, which fuse to form the neural tube
Neural tube, neural plate, neural groove, neural fold
Neural fold, notochord, neural plate, brain
Neural crest, neural tube, neural plate, spinal cord
mcqs.why: Notochordal cells induce overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate; its centre forms the neural groove and folds, whose cells fuse to form the neural tube.

mcqs.q: What does the neural tube differentiate into, and what is the embryo then called?
options: Heart and blood vessels; called a fetus
Placenta and membranes; called a morula
Digestive tract and lungs; called a gastrula
Brain and spinal cord; the embryo is designated as neurula when the tube forms
mcqs.why: The neural tube grows and differentiates into the brain and spinal cord, and at the point the tube pinches off the embryo is designated as the neurula.

mcqs.q: What is spina bifida?
options: Failure of the neural crest to migrate
Failure of the protective covering to close around the spinal cord, leaving a gap that can cause permanent nerve damage and sometimes paralysis
Failure of the heart to close the foramen ovale
Failure of the follicle to release an egg
mcqs.why: Failure of the protective covering to close around the spinal cord leaves a gap and causes spina bifida, which can lead to permanent nerve damage and sometimes paralysis.

mcqs.q: Where do neural crest cells arise, and why are they called the fourth germ layer?
options: From the region of the neural plate border; they migrate widely forming sensory nerves, sympathetic ganglia, parts of skull, teeth and many other parts
From the endoderm; they form the gut lining
From the trophoblast; they form the placenta
From the yolk sac; they form red blood cells
mcqs.why: Neural crest develops at the neural plate border and its cells migrate widely to form nerves, sympathetic ganglia, skull bone, teeth and many other parts, so many embryologists call it the fourth germ layer.

mcqs.q: What is organogenesis, and what is its first major step?
options: Formation of gametes; first step is fertilization
Increase in size and mass; first step is growth
Formation of organs and organ systems during embryonic development; first major step is neurulation
Formation of germ layers; first step is gastrulation
mcqs.why: Organogenesis is the stage where organs and organ systems form; its first major step is neurulation, the differentiation of ectoderm producing brain and spinal cord.

mcqs.q: When does growth begin in human development, and what is the embryo called from then until birth?
options: From the fourth week; called a neurula
From the 3rd week; called a gastrula
By the start of the third month; from the third month till birth it is called the fetus
mcqs.why: Growth begins by the start of the third month and ends long after birth; from the third month till birth the human embryo is called the fetus.

mcqs.q: By the end of the fourth week, what brain structures are formed?
options: The vesicles of fore, mid and hind brain
mcqs.why: At the end of the fourth week the vesicles of fore, mid and hind brain are formed, while all flexures become evident by the end of the eighth to ninth week.

mcqs.q: Do sensory and motor nerves have the same origin?
options: Yes, both arise from the neural tube
No: motor nerves arise from neural crest, sensory from brain
No: many motor nerves arise from the developing brain and spinal cord, but sensory nerves have a separate origin, the neural crest
Yes, both arise from neural crest
mcqs.why: Many motor nerves arise from the developing brain and spinal cord, but the sensory nerves have a separate origin, the neural crest at the neural plate border.

mcqs.q: Which part of the medulla do neural crest cells help to form?
options: The cortical region of medulla, along with skull bone and teeth
The medulla of the kidney only
The medulla oblongata of the brain only
mcqs.why: Neural crest cells also help in the formation of the cortical region of medulla, skull bone, teeth and many other parts, as stated in the notes.

lessons.title: Control of Development: Nucleus, Cytoplasm and Embryonic Induction
lessons.notes_html:
Every body cell of a multicellular organism contains a complete set of chromosomes with all bodily genes, produced by mitosis of the zygote. Yet cells differentiate along different lines: studies confirm that the nucleus determines the characteristics of the individual, while the cytoplasm selectively turns some genes on and switches others off.

21.2 Control of Development

21.2.1 Role of Nucleus in Development

  • Dietrich (1891) took a sea urchin zygote after one division and separated the two daughter cells; each grew into a complete, normal larva. He concluded that both cells contained all the genetic information of the original zygote.
  • Spemann, experiment 1 — He divided a salamander zygote into two equal halves with a minute ligature of human hair; the nucleus was in one half only. Cleavage was completed in the nucleated half but the enucleated half did not divide. When the nucleated side reached the 16-cell stage, one cleavage nucleus crossed the narrow cytoplasmic bridge to the enucleated side, which immediately started dividing; both sides completed cleavage and formed two complete embryos.
  • Spemann, experiment 2 — He separated the two halves of an embryo, both containing nuclei; both developed into complete embryos. Even a single cell separated from a 16-cell embryo contains a complete set of genes and can form a complete embryo.
  • Sometimes the nucleated half developed into an abnormal ball of cells: development depends on the position of the grey crescent, the pigment-free area that appears at the time of fertilization. In the half lacking the grey crescent, no further development can take place.

Spemann's conclusions: (i) the nuclear information is the same in each daughter cell; (ii) the grey crescent area in the cytoplasm contains information essential for proper development. Differentiation is caused in two ways: (i) cytoplasmic segregation of determinants during cleavage, and (ii) induction or interaction with neighbouring cells.

Role of Cytoplasm in Development

Different cytoplasmic components contain different morphogenetic determinants responsible for cell differentiation. In the zygote of an ascidian (urochordate), four different colours of cytoplasm are segregated into different blastomeres: clear cytoplasm produces larval epidermis; yellow cytoplasm gives rise to muscle cells; grey vegetal cytoplasm gives rise to gut; grey equatorial cytoplasm produces notochord and neural tube.

Experiment on Acetabularia

Acetabularia is a unicellular alga with a foot, stalk and umbrella-shaped cap, and a single nucleus in the foot. A. mediterranea has a regular-shaped cap and A. crenulata an irregular-shaped cap. Hammerling showed that if the cap is removed a new one is regenerated. He cut off the nucleus-containing base (foot) of one species and grafted a similar piece containing the nucleus of the other species; the new regenerated cap had the characters of the species whose nucleus was grafted. So the nucleus, not the stalk cytoplasm, determined the structure of the cap: genes express according to the type of nucleus. Overall, both gene and cytoplasm play an important role: the nucleus contains all the genes, while the cytoplasm controls that genes transcribe at their proper time.

21.2.2 Differentiation and Embryonic Induction

The capacity of some cells to evoke a specific developmental response in others is called embryonic induction. Spemann removed a piece of ectoderm from a salamander embryo and grew it separately: the donor embryo formed a defective nervous system and the isolated piece formed no structure at all. When he separated the mesoderm underlying the ectoderm, no nervous system developed — proving that mesoderm stimulates ectodermal cells to form the nervous system.

Hans Spemann and Hilde Mangold (1924) removed a piece of the dorsal lip of the blastopore from one salamander gastrula and transplanted it into a ventral or lateral position of another gastrula. It invaginated, developed a notochord and somites, and induced a second embryo with a neural tube and complete nervous system where the lip was placed. Only cells from the dorsal lip were capable of inducing a complete embryo; this area corresponds to the presumptive areas of notochord, somites and prechordal plate. Spemann designated the dorsal lip the primary organizer, and this was called primary induction. Many other cell types originate by later inductive interactions, called secondary induction, e.g. cells of the neural plate induce neural crest in the embryo.

Key Points

  • All cells carry the same nuclear information (Dietrich; Spemann's ligature experiments); even one cell of a 16-cell embryo can form a complete embryo.
  • The grey crescent of the cytoplasm holds information essential for proper development.
  • Acetabularia grafts (Hammerling) prove the nucleus determines characters such as cap shape.
  • Embryonic induction: one tissue evokes a specific response in another; the dorsal lip of the blastopore is the primary organizer (Spemann and Mangold, 1924).
  • Primary induction forms a secondary embryo; secondary induction covers later interactions such as neural plate inducing neural crest.

mcqs.q: What did Dietrich (1891) conclude from separating the two daughter cells of a sea urchin zygote?
options: Only one cell contained genetic information
Each cell grew into a complete normal larva, so both cells contained all the genetic information of the original zygote
mcqs.why: Dietrich separated the two daughter cells after one division and each grew into a complete normal larva, concluding both cells contained all genetic information of the zygote.

mcqs.q: In Spemann's ligature experiment, what happened when a nucleus crossed to the enucleated half at the 16-cell stage?
options: Only a ball of abnormal cells formed on both sides
The enucleated side immediately started dividing and both sides formed two complete embryos
mcqs.why: Cleavage occurred only in the nucleated half, but when one cleavage nucleus crossed the cytoplasmic bridge at the 16-cell stage, the enucleated side started dividing and both formed complete embryos.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the grey crescent in development?
options: This pigment-free area appearing at fertilization holds cytoplasmic information essential for proper development; a half lacking it cannot develop further
It is a pigment with no developmental role
It forms the neural tube directly
It determines only the skin colour of the larva
mcqs.why: Spemann found the half lacking the grey crescent, the pigment-free area appearing at fertilization, showed no further development, so it contains information essential for proper development.

mcqs.q: In the ascidian zygote, which cytoplasm gives rise to muscle cells and which to gut?
options: Clear cytoplasm gives muscle; yellow gives gut
Grey equatorial gives gut; clear gives muscle
Yellow cytoplasm gives rise to muscle cells; grey vegetal cytoplasm gives rise to gut
Yellow gives epidermis; grey vegetal gives notochord
mcqs.why: In the ascidian, clear cytoplasm produces larval epidermis, yellow cytoplasm gives muscle cells, grey vegetal cytoplasm gives gut, and grey equatorial cytoplasm produces notochord and neural tube.

mcqs.q: What did Hammerling's Acetabularia graft experiment prove?
options: The stalk cytoplasm determines cap shape
The nucleus determines the structure of the cap: a regenerated cap had the characters of the species whose nucleus was grafted
The cap can never regenerate after removal
Both species produce identical caps regardless of nucleus
mcqs.why: Hammerling grafted a nucleus-containing foot of one species onto another; the regenerated cap matched the nucleus donor species (regular in A. mediterranea, irregular in A. crenulata), proving the nucleus determines cap characters.

mcqs.q: Where is the single nucleus of Acetabularia located?
mcqs.why: Acetabularia is a unicellular alga with a foot, stalk and umbrella-shaped cap, and a single nucleus located in the foot, as used in Hammerling's grafts.

mcqs.q: What is embryonic induction?
options: The division of the zygote into blastomeres
The shortening of telomeres at each division
The fusion of sperm and egg membranes
The capacity of some cells to evoke a specific developmental response in other cells
mcqs.why: Embryonic induction is defined as the capacity of some cells to evoke a specific developmental response in others, for example mesoderm stimulating ectoderm to form the nervous system.

mcqs.q: What did Spemann and Mangold (1924) show with the dorsal lip transplant?
options: The dorsal lip formed no structure when transplanted
Only ventral lip cells could induce a complete embryo
A transplanted dorsal lip of the blastopore invaginated, formed notochord and somites, and induced a second embryo with a neural tube and complete nervous system; it is the primary organizer
mcqs.why: Spemann and Hilde Mangold transplanted the dorsal lip to a ventral or lateral position and it induced a second complete embryo, so Spemann designated the dorsal lip the primary organizer in primary induction.

mcqs.q: What is secondary induction? Give the example from the notes.
options: Dorsal lip inducing a whole second embryo
Later inductive interactions, e.g. cells of the neural plate induce neural crest in the embryo
mcqs.why: Secondary induction covers later inductive interactions after primary induction, for example cells of the neural plate inducing neural crest in the embryo.

mcqs.q: How is differentiation caused, according to the notes?
options: Only by changes in the nucleus of each cell
Only by hormones from the placenta
In two ways: cytoplasmic segregation of determinants during cleavage, and induction or interaction with neighbouring cells
mcqs.why: Differentiation is caused in two ways: cytoplasmic segregation of determinants during cleavage, and induction or interaction with neighbouring cells, while nuclear information stays the same.

lessons.title: Human Development: Fertilization, Implantation and the First Trimester
lessons.notes_html:
Soon after syngamy, fertilization occurs and the one-celled zygote is formed. The zygote undergoes changes that lead to the formation of the embryo, the fetus and ultimately an adult.

21.3 Human Embryonic Development

Fertilization (conception) normally takes place in the proximal portion of the fallopian tube, and the zygote travels down towards the uterus. In the tube it undergoes cleavage, forming a blastocyst (a cluster of cells resembling a tiny raspberry) by the time it reaches the uterus: 2-cell stage on day 1, 4-cell on day 2, early morula on day 3, advanced morula on day 4, blastocyst on day 6, and implantation in the uterine wall on days 7–10.

Pregnancy is usually established when the blastocyst is implanted (embedded) into the endometrium of the uterus. The inner cells of the blastocyst become the embryo, while the outer cells become the membranes that protect and nourish it. After implantation the embryo secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG), the pregnancy hormone recorded in a pregnancy test, which retains the corpus luteum so progesterone secretion continues (FSH is inhibited) and the endometrium is maintained and developed. The outer protective membrane, the chorion, surrounds the embryo, develops villi (fibrous projections) and burrows into the endometrium; later the placenta begins to form and nourishes the fetus throughout pregnancy.

A normal human pregnancy or gestation lasts nine months: 280 days from the time of the last menstruation, or 266 days after fertilization. Note: the book's Summary prints "266 days after last menstrual period", which mixes the two figures — 280 days is counted from the last menstrual period and 266 days from fertilization. The gestation period is divided into three trimesters (three-month periods).

21.3.1 Development of Human Fetus in First Trimester

The first trimester begins from the last menstrual period (LMP) and consists of fertilization, blastocyst formation, implantation, development of extra-embryonic membranes, placental development and major events of organogenesis. At the end of the second week the blastocyst is implanted in the endometrium and covered by endometrial cells, so the embryo gets nourishment directly from the endometrium. The outer layer of the blastocyst, the trophoblast, with the endometrium slowly gives rise to the placenta.

Extra-Embryonic Membranes and Placenta

  • Amnion — The first protective coat, the embryo's personal pond, filled with (amniotic) fluid that gives a watery medium and protects the fetus from physical trauma. The fluid surrounding the embryo is the amniotic fluid.
  • Allantois — The second protective coat; it contributes to the circulatory system and its blood vessels become the umbilical cord vessels that transport blood to and from the placenta.
  • Chorion — The third protective coat; it covers all other membranes and becomes part of the placenta.
  • Yolk sac — Contains little or no yolk in humans; it is the first site of RBC formation and also becomes part of the umbilical cord.

The placenta is a disc-like structure that closely attaches the embryo, through the umbilical cord, to the mother's blood vascular system. It exchanges glucose, amino acids, salts, CO₂ and urea between mother and fetus and produces estrogen and progesterone to maintain pregnancy. It grows throughout pregnancy, but the mother's blood supply to it is completed by the end of the first trimester (about 12–13 weeks); the corpus luteum then slowly degenerates as HCG declines and the placenta takes over progesterone production. At the end of the first trimester the fetus is fully formed, weighing about one ounce and measuring an average 3 to 4 inches in length.

StageMajor Events of the First Trimester
By the end of 4 weeksAll major systems and organs begin to form; embryo looks like a tadpole; neural tube, digestive system, heart and circulatory system begin; beginnings of eyes and ears; tiny limb buds appear; heart is beating
By the end of 8 weeksBody systems continue to develop; embryo takes a human shape with a large head; mouth, tooth buds, eyes, nose and ears become distinct; arms and legs clearly visible; fingers and toes webbed but distinguishable; heartbeat can be heard with a fetal Doppler; bones begin to develop; embryo in constant motion, not yet felt by the mother
Weeks 9 to 12After 8 weeks the embryo is called a fetus; at 1 to 1½ inches all major organs are formed; external genital organs develop; finger and toe nails appear; eyelids form; fetal movement increases; arms and legs fully formed; voice box (larynx) begins to form

The fetus is most vulnerable during the first 12 weeks, when all major organs are forming and can be damaged by drugs, radiation, tobacco and toxic chemicals; even so, by the end of 12 weeks the fetus cannot survive independently.

Key Points

  • Fertilization occurs in the fallopian tube; implantation into the endometrium (days 7–10) establishes pregnancy.
  • HCG from the embryo retains the corpus luteum so progesterone maintains the endometrium.
  • Gestation is 280 days from the last menstrual period (266 days from fertilization), divided into three trimesters.
  • Extra-embryonic membranes are amnion, allantois, chorion and yolk sac; the placenta exchanges materials and makes estrogen and progesterone.
  • By 4 weeks the heart beats; by 8 weeks the embryo looks human; after 8 weeks it is called a fetus.

mcqs.q: Where does fertilization normally take place, and when does implantation occur?
options: In the uterus; implantation on day 1
In the ovary; implantation on day 6
In the vagina; implantation on days 7-10
In the proximal portion of the fallopian tube; implantation in the uterine wall on days 7-10
mcqs.why: Fertilization normally takes place in the proximal portion of the fallopian tube, and the blastocyst implants in the uterine wall on days 7 to 10.

mcqs.q: What is the correct developmental timetable in the tube and uterus?
options: 2-cell on day 1, 4-cell on day 2, early morula day 3, advanced morula day 4, blastocyst day 6
mcqs.why: The notes give: 2-cell stage day 1, 4-cell day 2, early morula day 3, advanced morula day 4, blastocyst day 6, and implantation days 7-10.

mcqs.q: How long is normal human gestation counted from the last menstruation and from fertilization?
options: 280 days from the last menstruation; 266 days after fertilization
266 days from last menstruation; 280 days from fertilization
mcqs.why: A normal pregnancy lasts 280 days from the time of the last menstruation, or 266 days after fertilization; the difference is 280 minus 266 equals 14 days.

mcqs.q: What does HCG do after implantation?
options: It retains the corpus luteum so progesterone secretion continues, FSH is inhibited and the endometrium is maintained
mcqs.why: After implantation the embryo secretes human chorionic gonadotropin, which retains the corpus luteum so progesterone continues, FSH is inhibited and the endometrium is maintained and developed.

mcqs.q: Which membrane is the embryo's personal pond, and what does it do?
options: Chorion; it becomes part of the placenta
Allantois; its vessels become umbilical cord vessels
Yolk sac; first site of RBC formation
Amnion, filled with amniotic fluid giving a watery medium and protecting the fetus from physical trauma
mcqs.why: The amnion is the first protective coat, the embryo's personal pond filled with amniotic fluid that gives a watery medium and protects the fetus from physical trauma.

mcqs.q: What are the roles of the allantois and yolk sac in humans?
options: Allantois forms the placenta covering; yolk sac stores large yolk
Allantois contributes to the circulatory system and its vessels become umbilical cord vessels; yolk sac has little or no yolk and is the first site of RBC formation
mcqs.why: The allantois contributes to the circulatory system, its blood vessels becoming umbilical cord vessels, while the yolk sac contains little or no yolk and is the first site of RBC formation.

mcqs.q: What does the placenta exchange and produce?
options: It exchanges only oxygen and produces only HCG
It exchanges only waste products and produces prolactin
It exchanges glucose, amino acids, salts, carbon dioxide and urea between mother and fetus and produces estrogen and progesterone to maintain pregnancy
mcqs.why: The disc-like placenta exchanges glucose, amino acids, salts, CO2 and urea between mother and fetus and produces estrogen and progesterone to maintain pregnancy.

mcqs.q: By the end of the first trimester, what is the state of the fetus?
options: It is fully formed, weighing about one ounce and measuring an average 3 to 4 inches in length, but cannot survive independently
It weighs about 3400 grams and can survive independently
Only the neural tube has formed
mcqs.why: At the end of the first trimester the fetus is fully formed, weighing about one ounce and measuring 3 to 4 inches, yet by the end of 12 weeks it cannot survive independently.

mcqs.q: What has happened by the end of 4 weeks of development?
options: Fingers and toes are fully separate and nails appear
Sex can be determined by ultrasound
All major systems and organs begin to form; embryo looks like a tadpole; neural tube, heart and circulatory system begin; limb buds appear; heart is beating
mcqs.why: By the end of 4 weeks all major systems begin to form, the embryo looks like a tadpole, neural tube, digestive, heart and circulatory systems begin, limb buds appear and the heart is beating.

mcqs.q: When is the developing young one first called a fetus, and why is the first 12 weeks the most vulnerable period?
options: After 4 weeks; because the heart starts beating
After 8 weeks it is called a fetus; the first 12 weeks are most vulnerable because all major organs are forming and can be damaged by drugs, radiation, tobacco and toxic chemicals
At implantation; because the placenta forms
mcqs.why: After 8 weeks the embryo is called a fetus, with all major organs formed by 9-12 weeks; the fetus is most vulnerable during the first 12 weeks when organs forming can be damaged by drugs, radiation, tobacco and chemicals.

lessons.title: Second and Third Trimesters, Twins, Placenta and Umbilical Cord
lessons.notes_html:
After the first trimester, all major organs are already formed. The second and third trimesters are mainly periods of growth, maturation and preparation for birth.

Second Trimester

During the second trimester the fetus looks quite human and its sex becomes apparent and can be determined with the help of ultrasound. In girls the uterus and ovaries develop, while in males the testes begin to descend. The baby grows to about 0.6 kg and 0.3 metre long. The sensory organs are almost completely developed; the fetus can hear, and the eyelids and lashes are quite apparent. The heartbeat can be felt through a stethoscope. The head is about half of the overall body size. The mother can feel the movements of the fetus, and fingerprints begin to develop — fingerprints are unique to every individual; even identical twins have different fingerprints.

Third Trimester

The third trimester is a rapid growth period: body weight increases about 28 grams per day, i.e. it doubles several times. The eyes are open and subcutaneous fat begins to be deposited. At the end of this trimester the fetal head descends towards the cervix. After 9 months of pregnancy, at normal delivery, the baby might be about 18–20½ inches and weigh 6 to 9 pounds, or about 3400 grams. The lungs mature, the brain develops rapidly, and the fetus is fully formed and ready for birth.

21.3.2 Twins and Quadruplets

Two or more fetuses in one pregnancy are called multiple fetuses, either identical or non-identical (fraternal).

  • Identical twins or quadruplets come from a monozygote: a single ovum fertilized by one sperm. During the first, second or third cleavage the cells of the zygote separate and two, four or eight embryos are formed. All are of the same sex, blood type and most other features, though they do not always look exactly alike — fingerprints differ, and one may be right-handed while the other is left-handed. Identical twins mostly share the same placenta and chorion but usually grow in separate amniotic sacs.
  • Fraternal (non-identical) twins come from multiple fertilized eggs, i.e. they are dizygotic or multiple zygotic. They may be of the same sex or different sexes, their placenta and amniotic sacs are also separate, and they differ from each other in many features, sharing only about half their genes like ordinary siblings.

21.3.3 The Placenta and Umbilical Cord

The placenta was the source of nutrients and oxygen for the fetus and the site for removal of waste products from fetal circulation, because the fetal lungs were not functional as organs of gas exchange. The fetal body had two adaptations to limit blood flow to the lungs: the foramen ovale, a hole between the two atria, shunted most atrial blood directly into the left atrium, avoiding the right ventricle and pulmonary circulation; and the ductus arteriosus, a connection between the pulmonary artery and aorta, sent right ventricular blood into the aorta rather than through the lungs. At birth the foramen ovale is closed by two flaps of heart tissue that fold together and fuse; the ductus arteriosus is shut off by contraction of muscles in its walls, though complete closure may take several months, and the two umbilical arteries and one vein also close off.

The placenta consists of a fetal part (chorionic villi, which increase surface area for absorption) and a maternal part (projections from the endometrium). Its average weight is about 600 grams, 15–20 cm in diameter and 3 cm thick at the centre. The umbilical cord, also called the naval string, connects the embryo to the placenta. It normally contains one umbilical vein, which supplies oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta, and two umbilical arteries, which bring back deoxygenated, nutrient-depleted blood to the placenta; thus the fetal heart pumps only deoxygenated blood to the placenta.

21.3.4 Difference Between Gestation and Pregnancy

Gestation is the period of time between conception and parturition (birth), during which the young one grows and develops inside the mother's uterus. Gestational age is the common term used during pregnancy to describe how far along the pregnancy is; a normal pregnancy can range from 38 to 40 weeks, or 9 months.

Key Points

  • Second trimester: fetus looks human, sex can be determined by ultrasound, grows to about 0.6 kg and 0.3 m, heartbeat heard by stethoscope, mother feels movements.
  • Third trimester: rapid growth of about 28 g per day, fat deposited, head descends to the cervix; birth weight about 3400 g.
  • Identical twins are monozygotic (same sex, shared placenta and chorion); fraternal twins are dizygotic with separate placentae and sacs.
  • Foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the fetal lungs and close after birth.
  • The umbilical cord has two arteries and one vein; the placenta weighs about 600 g.

mcqs.q: What happens during the second trimester regarding the sex and size of the fetus?
options: Sex becomes apparent and can be determined by ultrasound; baby grows to about 0.6 kg and 0.3 metre long
Sex cannot be determined; fetus weighs 3400 grams
Sex becomes apparent only at birth; fetus weighs one ounce
Testes descend in girls and ovaries develop in boys
mcqs.why: In the second trimester the fetus looks quite human, its sex becomes apparent by ultrasound, and it grows to about 0.6 kg and 0.3 metre long, with heartbeat heard by stethoscope.

mcqs.q: A fetus gains about 28 grams per day in the third trimester. How much is that in one week?
mcqs.why: Working: 28 grams per day multiplied by 7 days equals 196 grams per week. The notes give the third trimester rapid growth rate as about 28 grams per day.

mcqs.q: What is the expected size and weight of the baby at normal delivery after 9 months?
options: About 18-20.5 inches and 6 to 9 pounds, or about 3400 grams
mcqs.why: At normal delivery after 9 months the baby might be about 18 to 20.5 inches and weigh 6 to 9 pounds, or about 3400 grams, with mature lungs and rapid brain development.

mcqs.q: How do identical twins arise?
options: From a monozygote: a single ovum fertilized by one sperm, whose cells separate during first, second or third cleavage to form two, four or eight embryos
From two sperms fertilizing one egg
From division of the placenta only
mcqs.why: Identical twins come from a monozygote, a single ovum fertilized by one sperm; separation during first, second or third cleavage forms two, four or eight embryos of the same sex and blood type.

mcqs.q: How do fraternal twins differ from identical twins?
options: They come from multiple fertilized eggs (dizygotic), may be same or different sex, have separate placenta and sacs, and share only about half their genes like ordinary siblings
They share the same placenta and all genes
They come from a single ovum
mcqs.why: Fraternal twins are dizygotic from multiple fertilized eggs, with separate placenta and amniotic sacs, possibly different sexes, sharing only about half their genes like ordinary siblings.

mcqs.q: Do identical twins have identical fingerprints?
options: Yes, and handedness is also always the same
No, fingerprints are unique to every individual; even identical twins have different fingerprints, and handedness may also differ
mcqs.why: Fingerprints begin to develop in the second trimester and are unique to every individual; even identical twins have different fingerprints and one may be right-handed while the other is left-handed.

mcqs.q: What is the function of the foramen ovale in the fetal heart?
options: It pumps blood to the placenta
It is a hole between the two atria shunting most atrial blood directly into the left atrium, avoiding the right ventricle and pulmonary circulation
It connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta
It supplies oxygenated blood from the placenta
mcqs.why: The foramen ovale is a hole between the two atria that shunts most atrial blood into the left atrium, avoiding the right ventricle and lungs, and it closes by tissue flaps at birth.

mcqs.q: What does the ductus arteriosus do, and what happens to it at birth?
options: It connects the two atria; it stays open for months
It carries blood from placenta to fetus; it becomes the umbilical vein
It connects the pulmonary artery and aorta, sending right ventricular blood into the aorta rather than through the lungs; at birth it is shut off by contraction of muscles in its walls
mcqs.why: The ductus arteriosus connects pulmonary artery to aorta so right ventricular blood enters the aorta rather than the lungs; at birth muscle contraction shuts it off, complete closure taking several months.

mcqs.q: What are the average weight and dimensions of the placenta?
options: About 600 grams, 15-20 cm in diameter and 3 cm thick at the centre
About 0.6 kg and 0.3 metre, same as second trimester fetus only
mcqs.why: The placenta, with fetal chorionic villi and maternal endometrial parts, has an average weight of about 600 grams, 15-20 cm in diameter and 3 cm thick at the centre.

mcqs.q: What vessels does the umbilical cord normally contain?
options: Two veins and one artery carrying oxygenated blood to the placenta
One umbilical vein supplying oxygenated nutrient-rich blood from the placenta, and two umbilical arteries bringing deoxygenated nutrient-depleted blood back to the placenta
Only one vein and one artery
mcqs.why: The umbilical cord normally contains one vein supplying oxygenated nutrient-rich blood from the placenta and two arteries returning deoxygenated blood, so the fetal heart pumps only deoxygenated blood to the placenta.

lessons.title: Birth, Premature Birth and Nursing
lessons.notes_html:
Birth is also called parturition or labour. Normally, towards the end of pregnancy the uterus becomes progressively more excitable and develops such strong rhythmical contractions that the baby is expelled.

21.4 Birth and Nursing

21.4.1 Role of Fetal and Maternal Hormones in Controlling Birth

For normal birth two things must happen: the muscles in the womb and abdominal wall have to contract, and the cervix needs to soften or increase in diameter. Estrogen and progesterone are secreted during pregnancy, but from the seventh month onward estrogen secretion becomes greater than progesterone secretion. Estrogen stimulates the myometrial cells of the uterus to form abundant oxytocin receptors; the myometrium becomes more irritable and weak, irregular uterine contractions begin — the Braxton Hicks contractions or false labour pains. False pains convert into real labour pains with the help of two other chemical signals:

  • Oxytocin — Secreted from the fetal pituitary gland (and the mother's posterior pituitary), it excites the uterus and causes contractions of the uterine myometrium.
  • Fetal ACTH — The fetal pituitary also secretes adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which stimulates the adrenal gland to release corticosteroids. These decrease progesterone production by the placenta and stimulate the fetal membranes to produce more prostaglandins, which increase the power of contraction.

These powerful contractions stimulate the mother's hypothalamus, which signals for oxytocin release by the mother's posterior pituitary gland. Thus true labour begins: a positive feedback mechanism releases more and more oxytocin, causing greater contractile force, and oxytocin is released in waves during labour. The process of labour has three steps: (1) cervix dilation — opening up and thinning of the cervix; (2) expulsion of the baby — strong continuous contractions force the fetus down and out of the uterus and vagina; (3) expulsion of the placenta soon after birth.

After delivery the umbilical cord is still attached to the baby. It is clamped artificially as early as 1 to 5 minutes after birth, and clamping is followed by cutting of the cord, which is painless due to the lack of any nerves. Following the birth, usually within 10–15 minutes, the placenta separates from the uterine wall and is expelled by uterine contractions through the birth canal; this expulsion is termed the afterbirth.

21.4.2 The Premature Birth

The book defines a premature (preterm) birth as birth at less than 27 weeks (6 months) of the gestational period, caused by many factors during the second and third trimesters: smoking and not getting good prenatal care; being overweight or underweight during pregnancy; high blood pressure, blood clotting disorders and diabetes mellitus; getting pregnant too soon after having a baby; and multiple births or a baby with certain defects. (Note: most medical sources call any birth before 37 weeks premature; 27 weeks is the book's figure.) The premature baby faces many complications: increased risk of infections, difficulty in maintaining body temperature, feeding problems and possible jaundice, breathing difficulty because the lungs are not fully developed, and long-term complications such as blindness and disturbance in hearing.

21.4.3 Colostrum, Lactation or Nursing

The secretion and yielding of milk by the mother after giving birth is called lactation. Initially the mammary glands produce a special yellow-coloured, lymph-like fluid known as colostrum, quite rich in antibodies (particularly IgA), with little fat and less lactose and globulin protein than milk. After 2 or 3 days, milk production begins by prolactin, secreted from the anterior pituitary under the influence of prolactin-releasing hormone; prolactin also prepares and enlarges the mammary glands for milk production and storage. Once the glands are filled with milk they synthesize the serotonin neurotransmitter, which slows down prolactin production. In the majority of cases, as soon as breast feeding stops, the mother's reproductive cycle begins again.

Role of oxytocin in the secretion of milk: sucking of the baby stimulates sensory receptors around the nipples; nerve impulses pass to the hypothalamus, which stimulates the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin. Oxytocin causes dilation of milk ducts within the mammary glands and thus promotes ejection (let-down) of milk. Nursing also helps the mother, because oxytocin causes uterine contraction — new mothers experience cramps in the uterus while nursing — returning the uterus to its pre-pregnant size.

Breast FeedingBottle-Feeding
Perfect balance of nutrients, high level of nutrientsNot efficiently utilized as breast milk; contents depend on proper preparation
Digested and absorbed easily, always at perfect temperatureSome babies have difficulty tolerating certain elements
Advantages: baby gets immunity; readily available at any time and place; creates affection of mother and child due to prolactin. Disadvantages: early breastfeeding may be uncomfortable; certain medication can interrupt itAdvantages: presence of mother is not necessary; but baby does not get immunity and there is no or less affection due to absence of prolactin. Disadvantages: preparation time varies and can be unhygienic; baby may not tolerate formula; bottles and mixing items must always be carried

Key Points

  • From the 7th month estrogen exceeds progesterone and induces oxytocin receptors; Braxton Hicks (false) pains become real pains.
  • Oxytocin and prostaglandins drive labour by positive feedback; labour has three steps: cervix dilation, expulsion of the baby, expulsion of the placenta (afterbirth, within 10–15 minutes).
  • The cord is clamped and cut 1 to 5 minutes after birth; cutting is painless as the cord has no nerves.
  • Colostrum is the first yellow fluid, rich in IgA antibodies; prolactin makes milk and oxytocin ejects it.
  • The book defines premature birth as before 27 weeks; its complications include infection, breathing difficulty and jaundice.

mcqs.q: How do estrogen and progesterone change from the seventh month of pregnancy, and what does estrogen do?
options: Progesterone exceeds estrogen and stops all contractions
Estrogen secretion becomes greater than progesterone; estrogen stimulates myometrial cells to form abundant oxytocin receptors, making the myometrium more irritable
Estrogen decreases progesterone receptors in the placenta only
mcqs.why: From the seventh month onward estrogen secretion becomes greater than progesterone; estrogen stimulates myometrial cells to form abundant oxytocin receptors and weak irregular Braxton Hicks contractions begin.

mcqs.q: What are Braxton Hicks contractions?
options: Powerful contractions that expel the baby
Contractions that expel the placenta after birth
Contractions of the mammary glands for milk ejection
Weak, irregular uterine contractions (false labour pains) that later convert into real labour pains
mcqs.why: Braxton Hicks contractions are the weak irregular uterine contractions called false labour pains, which convert into real labour pains with help from oxytocin and prostaglandin signals.

mcqs.q: What does fetal ACTH do in starting labour?
options: It stimulates the adrenal gland to release corticosteroids, which decrease progesterone production by the placenta and stimulate fetal membranes to produce more prostaglandins, increasing contraction power
It produces milk in the mammary glands
mcqs.why: Fetal ACTH from the fetal pituitary stimulates the adrenal gland to release corticosteroids that decrease placental progesterone and stimulate fetal membranes to produce prostaglandins, increasing contraction power.

mcqs.q: Why is labour described as a positive feedback mechanism?
options: Powerful contractions stimulate the mother's hypothalamus, signalling more oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary, causing greater contractile force, with oxytocin released in waves
Contractions reduce oxytocin release until birth stops
Each contraction weakens the next one
mcqs.why: Contractions stimulate the mother's hypothalamus for more oxytocin release by the posterior pituitary, causing greater force and more oxytocin in waves, which is positive feedback driving true labour.

mcqs.q: What are the three steps of labour in order?
options: Expulsion of placenta, cervix dilation, expulsion of baby
Expulsion of baby, expulsion of placenta, cervix dilation
Cervix dilation, expulsion of the baby, expulsion of the placenta
Milk ejection, cervix dilation, expulsion of baby
mcqs.why: Labour has three steps: first cervix dilation with opening and thinning, second expulsion of the baby by strong continuous contractions, third expulsion of the placenta soon after birth.

mcqs.q: When is the umbilical cord clamped and cut, and why is cutting painless?
options: After 10-15 minutes; because the mother is anaesthetized
As early as 1 to 5 minutes after birth; cutting is painless due to lack of any nerves in the cord
Before birth; because the cord has no blood vessels
After one day; because the cord has dried
mcqs.why: After delivery the cord is clamped artificially as early as 1 to 5 minutes after birth and then cut; cutting is painless due to the lack of any nerves in the cord.

mcqs.q: When is the placenta expelled after birth, and what is this called?
options: Immediately before the baby; called dilation
Usually within 10-15 minutes after birth, expelled by uterine contractions through the birth canal; called the afterbirth
mcqs.why: Following birth, usually within 10 to 15 minutes, the placenta separates from the uterine wall and is expelled by uterine contractions; this expulsion is termed the afterbirth.

mcqs.q: How does the book define premature birth, and what is one complication?
options: Birth at less than 27 weeks (6 months) of gestation; complications include breathing difficulty because lungs are not fully developed, infections and jaundice
Birth before 37 weeks; complication is high birth weight
Birth after 40 weeks; complication is jaundice only
mcqs.why: The book defines premature birth as birth at less than 27 weeks, with complications including infection risk, temperature and feeding problems, jaundice and breathing difficulty from underdeveloped lungs.

mcqs.q: What is colostrum?
options: Mature milk produced after one month
A hormone from the posterior pituitary
A special yellow-coloured lymph-like fluid produced initially by mammary glands, quite rich in antibodies particularly IgA, with little fat and less lactose and globulin than milk
mcqs.why: Colostrum is the first yellow lymph-like fluid from the mammary glands, rich in IgA antibodies, with little fat and less lactose and globulin protein than milk; true milk production begins after 2-3 days.

mcqs.q: What are the separate roles of prolactin and oxytocin in nursing?
options: Prolactin ejects milk; oxytocin makes milk

Prolactin, from the anterior pituitary, makes milk and enlarges mammary glands; oxytocin, from the posterior pituitary after sucking signals, dilates milk ducts and promotes ejection (let-down) of milk
mcqs.why: Prolactin secreted from the anterior pituitary produces milk after 2-3 days, while sucking triggers hypothalamus and posterior pituitary oxytocin release that dilates ducts and ejects milk, also contracting the uterus.

lessons.title: Disorders During Embryonic Development and Fetal Surgery
lessons.notes_html:
The fetus faces many disorders at birth, collectively known as embryonic development disorders or birth defects. The study of abnormal development is called teratology.

21.5 Disorders During Embryonic Development

21.5.1 Maternal Derived Abnormalities

These abnormalities are transmitted from mother to fetus during pregnancy or just after birth, such as rubella, neural tube defects, thyroid gland and limb development defects.

  • Rubella — Caused by the rubella virus and also called German measles. It is extremely dangerous if the mother is infected within the first twenty weeks of pregnancy: the baby may be born with Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS), comprising cardiac defects (patent ductus arteriosus), cerebral defects, ophthalmic defects (cataract) and deafness. It may also cause prematurity, low birth weight, anaemia and hepatitis.
  • Neural Tube Defects (NTDs) — Serious birth defects, from mild to severe impairment, due to abnormal closure of the neural fold, caused by incomplete development of the brain, spinal cord and meninges; the fetal spine fails to close properly during the early stages of pregnancy (spina bifida is one such defect).
  • Thyroid gland disorder — Congenital hypothyroidism of the newborn baby. The baby frequently has hyperbilirubinemia and delayed skeletal maturation, reflecting immaturity of liver and bone respectively, and is at risk of permanent mental retardation if thyroid hormone therapy is delayed or inadequate. Birth size, however, is normal.
  • Developmental (limb) defects — The upper and lower limbs have a large number of genetic and environment-derived abnormalities, some surgically repairable; partial or complete absence of limbs or digits is common.

21.5.2 Genetic Abnormalities Related to Spontaneous Abortions

Approximately 50% of first and second trimester miscarriages (spontaneous abortions) are due to a chromosome abnormality in the fetus. An extra chromosome (2n+1) or a missing chromosome (2n−1) can cause miscarriage, or lead to a child with learning difficulties, mental retardation and birth defects. These defects result from a mistake in cell division soon after conception — a random event that can occur in anyone's pregnancy. An inherited problem can also cause miscarriage: a parent may have a rearrangement (translocation) in which the chromosomes are structured differently. Another genetic cause is a change in a single gene or several genes on the chromosomes, causing specific genetic diseases or birth defects.

21.5.3 Fetal Surgery and Defected Fetal Development Problems

The surgery of the fetus within the maternal uterus to treat a prenatal defect is called fetal surgery. It helps correct detected fetal developmental problems before birth.

  • Open fetal surgery — The uterus is completely opened to operate on the fetus. It is done to treat or close neural tube defects and congenital diseases such as diaphragmatic hernia (an abnormal opening in the diaphragm, so organs move from the belly to the chest cavity near the lungs).
  • Minimally invasive foetoscopic surgery — Uses small incisions, guided by foetoscopy and sonography. It is used for fetal bladder outlet obstruction (blockage of the bladder), pulmonary/aortic valvuloplasty (widening of a stenotic aortic valve using a balloon catheter inside the valve) and atrial septostomy (a small hole created between the atria of the heart).

Key Points

  • Rubella (German measles) in the first 20 weeks can cause Congenital Rubella Syndrome: heart, brain, eye (cataract) defects and deafness.
  • Neural tube defects come from abnormal closure of the neural fold; congenital hypothyroidism risks mental retardation if treatment is delayed.
  • About 50% of early miscarriages are due to chromosome abnormalities (2n+1 or 2n−1), translocations or gene changes.
  • Fetal surgery treats defects before birth: open surgery for neural tube defects and diaphragmatic hernia; foetoscopic surgery for bladder obstruction, valvuloplasty and atrial septostomy.
  • Teratology is the study of abnormal development.

mcqs.q: What is teratology?
options: The study of normal embryonic development
Surgery of the fetus in the uterus
mcqs.why: Teratology is defined in the notes as the study of abnormal development; birth defects are collectively called embryonic development disorders.

mcqs.q: Why is rubella infection in the first twenty weeks of pregnancy extremely dangerous?
options: It causes only a mild rash in the mother
The baby may be born with Congenital Rubella Syndrome: cardiac defects (patent ductus arteriosus), cerebral defects, ophthalmic defects (cataract) and deafness
It causes premature birth only after 37 weeks
It affects only the mother's thyroid gland
mcqs.why: Rubella, or German measles, in the first 20 weeks can cause Congenital Rubella Syndrome with heart, brain and eye (cataract) defects and deafness, plus prematurity, low birth weight, anaemia and hepatitis.

mcqs.q: What causes neural tube defects?
options: Abnormal closure of the neural fold, from incomplete development of the brain, spinal cord and meninges; the fetal spine fails to close properly (spina bifida is one such defect)
mcqs.why: Neural tube defects are serious birth defects due to abnormal closure of the neural fold and incomplete development of brain, spinal cord and meninges; spina bifida is one such defect.

mcqs.q: What is true about a baby with congenital hypothyroidism?
options: Birth size is much smaller than normal
There is no risk to mental development
Birth size is normal, but there is hyperbilirubinemia and delayed skeletal maturation, with risk of permanent mental retardation if thyroid hormone therapy is delayed or inadequate
mcqs.why: In congenital hypothyroidism birth size is normal, but hyperbilirubinemia and delayed skeletal maturation reflect liver and bone immaturity, and delayed therapy risks permanent mental retardation.

mcqs.q: About what proportion of first and second trimester miscarriages are due to a chromosome abnormality in the fetus?
mcqs.why: Approximately 50 percent of first and second trimester miscarriages (spontaneous abortions) are due to a chromosome abnormality in the fetus, such as an extra (2n+1) or missing (2n-1) chromosome.

mcqs.q: What do 2n+1 and 2n-1 mean as genetic abnormalities?
options: Two extra sets of chromosomes and two missing sets
Normal diploid numbers with no effect
Changes in a single gene only
An extra chromosome (2n+1) or a missing chromosome (2n-1), which can cause miscarriage or a child with learning difficulties, mental retardation and birth defects
mcqs.why: An extra chromosome is written 2n+1 and a missing chromosome 2n-1; these result from a mistake in cell division soon after conception and can cause miscarriage or birth defects.

mcqs.q: What is a translocation as a cause of miscarriage?
options: A change in a single gene only
An inherited rearrangement in a parent in which the chromosomes are structured differently
A failure of the neural fold to close
An infection transmitted from mother to fetus
mcqs.why: An inherited problem causing miscarriage is a parental rearrangement called translocation, in which the chromosomes are structured differently; single or multiple gene changes are another genetic cause.

mcqs.q: What is fetal surgery?
options: Surgery on the mother after birth
