lessons.title: Acid Rain and Ozone Depletion
lessons.notes_html:
Two further results of human activity are acid rain, which damages soil, water, buildings and health, and ozone depletion, which removes Earth's shield against ultraviolet radiation.

25.5.3 Acid Rain

Acid rain, or acid deposition, is a broad term that includes any form of precipitation that contains acidic components such as sulphuric acid or nitric acid. The precipitation is not necessarily wet or liquid: the definition includes snow, fog and hail. The type of acid rain that contains water is called wet deposition, while acid rain that contains dust or gases is called dry deposition.

Causes of acid rain: acid rain may fall hundreds of miles away from the source of pollution. It is a natural phenomenon caused by chemicals emitted during volcanic eruptions and forest fires. However, the majority of acid rain is caused by human activity, such as the burning of coal by electricity generating plants, industrial boilers and large smelters that obtain metals from ores, which release sulphur dioxide (SO₂); in addition, nitrogen oxides (NOx) are emitted by automobiles. The causes of acid rain due to human activities are called anthropogenic sources. These gases react with water vapour in the atmosphere to form the acids.

Effects of acid rain:

  • It increases soil acidity.
  • It damages life in farms and forests.
  • It kills aquatic organisms and prevents their successful reproduction.
  • It increases the quantity of certain metals, such as aluminium, that may prove toxic to many organisms in the ecosystem.
  • It causes extensive damage to buildings and stone structures, known as stone cancer.
  • It adversely affects the nervous, respiratory and digestive systems of man.

25.5.4 Ozone Depletion

The ozone layer protects all life from the Sun's harmful radiations. The Earth's atmosphere is composed of several layers: the lower layer is the troposphere (10 km altitude) and the next layer is the stratosphere (10-50 km). The ozone layer is concentrated in 15-30 km above the Earth's surface in the stratosphere and contains O₃ molecules. Ozone is constantly being formed and broken down in the high atmosphere. Today there is widespread concern that the ozone layer is deteriorating due to the release of pollution containing the chemicals chlorine and fluorine.

Composition of the ozone layer: ozone is a bluish, explosive and highly poisonous gas. In the stratosphere, the normal concentration of ozone is about 0.1 part per million (ppm), compared with 0.02 ppm in the lower atmosphere. The ozone hole is not technically a hole where no ozone is present, but a region of depleted ozone in the stratosphere over the Antarctic that appears at the beginning of Southern Hemisphere spring (August-October). The average concentration of ozone in the atmosphere is about 300 Dobson Units; any area where the concentration drops below 220 Dobson Units is considered part of the ozone hole. In 1985 it was discovered that springtime levels of stratospheric ozone over Antarctica had declined by over 40% since 1977.

Formation of the ozone layer: ozone is formed in the atmosphere when ultraviolet radiation from the Sun splits one oxygen molecule into two oxygen atoms; the atomic oxygen then combines with another oxygen molecule to form ozone (O₃).

Causes of ozone layer depletion: in the stratosphere there is a group of commercially important compounds called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). They have been used as propellants in aerosol cans, as coolants (e.g. Freon) in air conditioners and refrigerators, as foam (e.g. Styrofoam) for insulation and packing, and as cleaners in the electronic industry. Ultraviolet radiation breaks CFCs and similar compounds into chlorine, fluorine and carbon. As CFCs rise to the atmosphere, the ultraviolet rays release chlorine. Under certain stratospheric conditions, chlorine and fluorine react with ozone, converting it into molecular oxygen (O₂) and atomic oxygen (O), so the ozone layer is thinned and the ozone hole develops over Antarctica.

Role of the ozone layer in protecting life on Earth: ozone molecules in the stratosphere absorb incoming solar ultraviolet radiations, protecting life on Earth from harmful UV rays.

Effects of ultraviolet radiation on human health: with depletion of the ozone layer, UV radiations reach the Earth's surface. Excessive exposure to UV radiation is linked to a number of human health problems, including sunburn, premature aging of skin, skin cancer and cataracts. Photosynthesis by phytoplankton is also affected and reduced by ultraviolet radiation, and increased UV harms crops, aquatic life and the immune system.

Key Points

  • Acid rain (acid deposition) contains sulphuric or nitric acid and falls as wet deposition (rain, snow, fog, hail) or dry deposition (dust, gases).
  • Most acid rain is anthropogenic: SO₂ from burning coal in power plants, boilers and smelters, and NOx from automobiles; it can fall hundreds of miles from the source.
  • Acid rain increases soil acidity, kills aquatic organisms, damages farms, forests and buildings (stone cancer) and harms human health.
  • The ozone layer (O₃) lies in the stratosphere, concentrated at 15-30 km, and absorbs harmful UV radiation.
  • CFCs release chlorine under UV radiation, which destroys ozone; the ozone hole forms over Antarctica, increasing skin cancer and cataracts.

mcqs.why: Acid rain causes extensive damage to buildings and stone structures, known as stone cancer, besides increasing soil acidity and killing aquatic organisms.

options: Below 220 Dobson Units (average is about 300 Dobson Units)
mcqs.why: Average atmospheric ozone is about 300 Dobson Units; any area where concentration drops below 220 Dobson Units is considered part of the ozone hole over Antarctica.

mcqs.why: In 1985 it was discovered that springtime levels of stratospheric ozone over Antarctica had declined by over 40% since 1977, forming the seasonal ozone hole.

lessons.title: Environmental Resources, Energy Sources and Protection of Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Wherever humans have gone, they have altered the environment according to their needs. The future of mankind depends on the protection and conservation of environmental resources.

25.6 Environmental Resources and their Depletion

Living organisms are important natural resources.

25.6.1 Kinds of Natural Resources

All resources of the environment can be divided into two groups: renewable and non-renewable resources.

  • Renewable resources — Un-exhaustible resources that replace themselves quickly enough to keep pace with consumption. Examples are air, water, land and wild life. Living organisms use these resources continuously, but they are constantly replaced by natural cycles, e.g. the water cycle, carbon cycle, oxygen cycle and nitrogen cycle.
  • Non-renewable resources — Resources formed at a rate much slower than their environmental consumption. They are exhaustible and cannot be replaced if destroyed. Examples are various metals, non-metallic minerals, coal, oil and natural gas.
Renewable ResourcesNon-Renewable Resources
Replace themselves quickly; un-exhaustibleForm much slower than they are used; exhaustible
Air, water, land, wild lifeMetals, minerals, coal, oil, natural gas
Replaced by natural cyclesCannot be replaced once destroyed

25.6.2 Conventional and Non-Conventional Energy Sources

Conventional energy sources are energy sources used for a long time: fossil fuels (coal, natural gas, oil), firewood, wood, peat and uranium. Fossil fuels provide 95% of the energy requirement and are non-renewable — they are the remains of plants and animals that lived millions of years ago. Humans prefer conventional sources because they are inexpensive and use established technologies that produce energy around the clock. Their disadvantages are a limited supply and that burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, etc.) and contributes to acid rain and pollution.

Non-conventional energy sources are continuously replenished by natural processes and are not commonly used. They include solar energy, hydro-electric energy (dams in rivers), wind, tidal and ocean wave energy, geothermal energy (heat from deep under the ground), ocean thermal power, biomass, bio-fuel (ethanol from plants) and bio-gas; they are also called renewable energy sources. They are abundant, pollution-free and eco-friendly, but can be inconsistent and costly to operate. In Pakistan, non-conventional sources are wind energy, hydroelectric power, solar energy and biogas.

Conventional SourcesNon-Conventional Sources
Used for a long time; inexpensive, established technologyNewer and less commonly used; continuously replenished
Fossil fuels, firewood, peat, uraniumSolar, wind, hydro-electric, tidal, geothermal, biomass, bio-gas
Limited supply; release greenhouse gasesAbundant and pollution-free, but inconsistent and costly to operate

Depletion of Resources

Resource depletion is the exhaustion of raw materials within a region; use of resources beyond their rate of replacement is considered resource depletion. Causes of resource depletion include over-consumption (excessive or unnecessary use of resources), non-equitable distribution of resources, overpopulation, slash-and-burn agricultural practices, technological and industrial development, erosion, irrigation, mining for oil and minerals, and pollution or contamination of resources.

25.6.3 Protection of Environmental Resources

Our health and well-being are closely linked to the quality of our air, water, soil and biological resources. We can protect them by reusing and recycling, educating the common masses, conserving resources, using renewable resources for energy, and planting trees.

Role of Government: the government controls and develops forests, dams, irrigation systems, power stations, roads, mines and industries. The Ministry of Environment plans and coordinates environment and forestry programmes: conservation and survey of flora, fauna, forests and wildlife, prevention and control of pollution, afforestation and regeneration of degraded areas. Environmental impact is assessed before any project that can damage the environment. Earth Day on 22nd April and tree plantation week are observed every year to educate the people. The book's example is the Tsunami Billion Tree Scheme, launched in 2014 by the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK), restoring 350,000 hectares of forests and degraded land.

Role of Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs): NGOs play a very important role in environmental protection and in creating mass awareness of problems caused by neglect and uncontrolled exploitation of natural resources; some work in awareness, others in research. Pakistan faces deforestation, air pollution, climate change, pesticide misuse and desertification, and the government alone cannot tackle these efficiently. Well-known organizations named in the unit include the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF).

Key Points

  • Renewable resources (air, water, land, wild life) replace themselves through natural cycles; non-renewable resources (coal, oil, gas, metals, minerals) form far slower than they are used.
  • Conventional energy sources have been used for a long time — fossil fuels provide 95% of energy needs; non-conventional sources (solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biomass) are renewable and cleaner.
  • Resource depletion is caused by over-consumption, overpopulation, unequal distribution, slash-and-burn farming, industry, mining and pollution.
  • Protection needs reuse and recycling, conservation, tree planting, government action through the Ministry of Environment, and NGO awareness work (IUCN, WWF).

options: Various metals, non-metallic minerals, coal, oil and natural gas
mcqs.why: Non-renewable resources are formed at a rate much slower than consumption and cannot be replaced if destroyed; examples are metals, minerals, coal, oil and natural gas.

mcqs.q: Fossil fuels provide about what percentage of the energy requirement?
mcqs.why: Fossil fuels provide 95% of the energy requirement and are non-renewable, being remains of plants and animals that lived millions of years ago.

options: Solar, wind, tidal and geothermal only
Fossil fuels (coal, natural gas, oil), firewood, wood, peat and uranium
mcqs.why: Conventional sources are used for a long time: fossil fuels, firewood, wood, peat and uranium, preferred because they are inexpensive and use established technologies.

mcqs.q: Non-conventional energy sources are also called what, and share which advantage?
options: Renewable energy sources; they are abundant, pollution-free and eco-friendly
Conventional sources; they release greenhouse gases
Fossil sources; they operate around the clock cheaply
mcqs.why: Non-conventional sources such as solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal and biomass are also called renewable energy sources, abundant and pollution-free, though inconsistent and costly.

options: Wind energy, hydroelectric power, solar energy and biogas
mcqs.why: In Pakistan, non-conventional sources are wind energy, hydroelectric power, solar energy and biogas, as listed in the notes for this lesson.

options: Exhaustion of raw materials within a region; use beyond the rate of replacement

options: Mining for oil and minerals and pollution
mcqs.why: Causes include over-consumption, non-equitable distribution, overpopulation, slash-and-burn farming, industry, erosion, irrigation, mining and pollution; reuse and recycling protect resources instead.

mcqs.why: Earth Day on 22nd April and tree plantation week are observed every year to educate the people, alongside Ministry of Environment programmes.

options: 350,000 hectares of forests and degraded land
mcqs.why: The Tsunami Billion Tree Scheme, launched in 2014 by the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, restored 350,000 hectares of forests and degraded land, the book's protection example.

lessons.title: Cloning of Genes Through Recombinant DNA Technology
lessons.notes_html:
Biotechnology is any technique that uses living organisms to make products. It was used as far back as biblical times — yeast to bake bread, ferment wine and make cheese. In 1862, Louis Pasteur discovered that fermentation is caused by micro-organisms, not an inorganic chemical process. After Mendel's work was rediscovered in 1900, geneticists made advances that led to the new era of DNA technology: genes can now be removed from one organism and inserted into another to produce insulin, growth hormone, drugs and vaccines, clean up pollutants, kill insect pests and increase soil fertility. This unit deals with genetic engineering — the manipulation or alteration of the genetic material of an organism.

26.1 Cloning of Genes

Cloning of genes produces many identical copies (clones) of a single gene. There are two ways of cloning a gene: recombinant DNA technology and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Recombinant DNA technology is used when a very large quantity of a gene is required, while PCR is used to create an optimum number of copies in a test tube in the laboratory. Cloning is a technique for developing a large number of genes, identical cells, tissues or organisms.

26.1.1 Gene Cloning through Recombinant DNA Technology

Recombinant DNA technology, popularly called genetic engineering, is a series of procedures used to join together (recombine) two or more segments of DNA from different sources. The recombinant DNA (rDNA) is also called chimeric DNA. To produce recombinant DNA, these components are required:

  • The gene of interest (desired gene) to be cloned.
  • Molecular scissors (restriction endonuclease) to cut out the gene of interest.
  • A vector or molecular carrier to carry the gene of interest.
  • The enzyme ligase, which forms the phosphodiester linkage between two adjacent nucleotides.
  • An expression system (such as bacteria) in which the gene, along with the vector, is inserted to get a large number of desired genes or specific chemical products.

26.1.2 Role of Molecular Scissors and DNA Ligase

Molecular scissors are restriction endonucleases, natural enzymes of bacteria first isolated by Hamilton D. Smith (1970) at John Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, USA. He observed that the enzyme cuts viral DNA to prevent replication of viral DNA in bacteria. Different species of bacteria produce different restriction endonucleases, which cut DNA at a very specific sequence of four to eight nucleotides arranged symmetrically in reverse order. Such sequences are called palindromic sequences and their cutting points are restriction sites. Over 3,000 restriction enzymes have been studied in detail and more than 600 are available commercially (230 different DNA sequences); about twenty are frequently used in recombinant DNA technology. Restriction enzymes are named after their host of origin.

EcoRI (isolated from Escherichia coli) is the most commonly used restriction enzyme. It cuts double-stranded DNA so that single-stranded complementary ends are left, with (AATT) bases at the cleavage site of its palindromic sequence (GAATTC in the book's Fig. 26.1). These complementary ends are called sticky ends (a staggered cut) because they bind by complementary base pairing, so foreign DNA with the same palindromic sequence is easily inserted into vector DNA.

Gene of Interest

The desired gene can be acquired in three ways:

  • Isolated from the chromosomes by cutting at the flanking sites of the gene with restriction endonucleases (enzymes bacteria use for their own protection against viruses — they cut viral DNA but do not harm the bacterial chromosome).
  • Synthesized in the laboratory from mRNA using reverse transcriptase, naturally found in retroviruses; this DNA is called complementary DNA (cDNA).
  • If the gene is small, synthesized artificially by a machine called a DNA synthesizer, which creates DNA molecules of a desired nucleotide sequence.

Role of Molecular Carriers or Vectors

A vector acts as a vehicle for carrying foreign DNA into a host cell for multiplication. A common vector is a plasmid — a small extra-chromosomal circular DNA molecule in bacteria, containing genes for antibiotic resistance and fertility, etc. Commonly used vectors are plasmids, lambda phage DNA, yeast artificial chromosomes (YACs) and bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs).

DNA Ligase

DNA ligase acts as molecular glue: it seals the foreign pieces of DNA into the vector to form recombinant or chimeric DNA. The complementary ends of two DNA molecules are joined by hydrogen bonding, and ligase forms the phosphodiester linkage between adjacent nucleotides.

Key Points

  • Biotechnology uses living organisms to make products; genetic engineering alters genetic material.
  • Genes are cloned by recombinant DNA technology (large quantities) or PCR (copies in a test tube).
  • Restriction endonucleases are molecular scissors; Hamilton D. Smith first isolated them in 1970.
  • They cut at palindromic restriction sites of 4-8 nucleotides, leaving sticky ends; EcoRI is the commonest example.
  • A gene of interest is obtained by isolation, from mRNA as cDNA, or by a DNA synthesizer.
  • Vectors (plasmids, lambda phage, YACs, BACs) carry the gene; DNA ligase is the molecular glue that seals it in.

mcqs.q: What is biotechnology, as defined in the notes?
options: Any technique that uses living organisms to make products
Any technique that uses machines to copy DNA
The study of fossils and evolution only
The chemical synthesis of drugs without organisms
mcqs.why: The notes define biotechnology as any technique that uses living organisms to make products, an old practice now extended by DNA technology.

mcqs.q: Who discovered in 1862 that fermentation is caused by micro-organisms?
mcqs.why: Louis Pasteur discovered in 1862 that fermentation is caused by micro-organisms, not by an inorganic chemical process.

mcqs.q: When was Mendel's work rediscovered, leading towards the new era of DNA technology?
mcqs.why: After Mendel's work was rediscovered in 1900, geneticists made the advances that led to the new era of DNA technology.

mcqs.q: Recombinant DNA is also called what?
mcqs.why: Recombinant DNA, formed by joining DNA segments from different sources, is also called chimeric DNA in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which component cuts out the gene of interest in recombinant DNA technology?
mcqs.why: Molecular scissors, the restriction endonucleases, cut out the gene of interest; ligase joins and the vector carries it.

mcqs.q: What does DNA ligase do in recombinant DNA formation?
options: It forms the phosphodiester linkage between adjacent nucleotides
It cuts DNA at restriction sites
It carries DNA into a host cell
It copies DNA in a test tube
mcqs.why: DNA ligase acts as molecular glue, forming the phosphodiester linkage between two adjacent nucleotides to seal DNA pieces together.

mcqs.q: Who first isolated restriction endonucleases, and in which year?
mcqs.why: Restriction endonucleases were first isolated by Hamilton D. Smith in 1970 at John Hopkins University in Baltimore, USA.

mcqs.q: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at palindromic sequences of how many nucleotides?
mcqs.why: The notes state these enzymes cut at very specific sequences of four to eight nucleotides arranged symmetrically in reverse order.

mcqs.q: EcoRI leaves single-stranded complementary ends with which bases at the cleavage site?
mcqs.why: EcoRI cuts double-stranded DNA leaving sticky ends with AATT bases at the cleavage site of its palindromic sequence GAATTC.

mcqs.q: DNA made in the laboratory from mRNA using reverse transcriptase is called what?
mcqs.why: DNA synthesized from mRNA using reverse transcriptase, naturally found in retroviruses, is called complementary DNA or cDNA.

lessons.title: Expression of Recombinant DNA, Gene Delivery and Gene Validation
lessons.notes_html:
Once a gene of interest has been sealed into a vector, the recombinant DNA must enter a living system that will multiply it and express it as a product. This lesson completes section 26.1.2: the expression system, the cut-copy-paste steps for creating recombinant DNA, the techniques that deliver genes into cells, and how successful transformants are validated (selected).

Expression of Recombinant DNA / Expression System

The most suitable organism to multiply and express recombinant DNA is bacteria, because they have a short generation time and a simple genetic system. Bacterial cells easily take up recombinant plasmid, especially if treated with calcium chloride to make them more permeable. As the bacterium reproduces, each daughter bacterium contains the gene of interest, which expresses itself and makes a product, e.g. in Agrobacterium tumefaciens.

Steps for Creation of Recombinant DNA (Plasmid)

The simplified steps for creating a recombinant DNA and a transgenic species are cut, copy and paste:

  • 1. Cut: A gene of interest is removed from the cell of an organism using molecular scissors.
  • 2. Copy: Multiple copies are made (gene cloning), usually in bacteria (sometimes phage), e.g. Escherichia coli is the regulating system.
  • 3. Paste: The genes are inserted (pasted) into a bacterium, an egg cell or a plant cell of another species and (after fertilization in the case of an animal) become part of the newly formed transgenic organism's DNA.
  • 4. The transgenic organism develops into a mature organism with the new gene 'switched on' to function.

Transformation of Expressing System / Gene Delivery Techniques

  • Agrobacterium-mediated transformation — bacteria take up recombinant plasmid, especially after calcium chloride treatment makes them more permeable; as the cell reproduces, a bacterial clone forms and each new cell contains at least one plasmid.
  • Micro-injection — in animals, DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an egg, usually under an optical microscope, when creating transgenic species.
  • Electroporation — high-voltage electric shocks increase membrane permeability to introduce DNA into cells.
  • Biolistics — delivery of nucleic acid (recombinant genes) into plant cells by high-speed particle bombardment; DNA-coated metal particles are propelled by a gene gun.
  • Vectors — DNA may be carried by an adenovirus, a liposome or a bacterial plasmid into cells; it either enters directly into blood or may be delivered by aerosol (nasal or oral). Liposomes are minute spherical sacs of molecules enclosing a water droplet, carrying genes or drugs.

Gene Validation

For a bacterial clone: a particular antibiotic is added to the transformed clone; if the clone has resistance against the antibiotic, it remains alive and continues to grow. Important antibiotic markers are ampicillin (the book prints 'Ampiciline'), kanamycin (printed 'Kalamycine') and streptomycin, etc.

For animal and plant cells: a gene for a fluorescent protein from jellyfish is now used to determine whether an individual has successfully incorporated a transgenic gene. The fluorescent gene is used as a marker, attached to the gene of interest that will be inserted into the prospective transgenic organism, so the resulting offspring (cell) gives fluorescence under certain lighting conditions.

Key Points

  • Bacteria are the main expression system: short generation time, simple genetics, and calcium chloride makes them permeable to plasmids.
  • Creating recombinant DNA is cut (remove the gene), copy (clone it, usually in bacteria) and paste (insert it into another species).
  • Gene delivery methods: Agrobacterium-mediated transformation, micro-injection, electroporation, biolistics and vectors such as adenovirus, liposomes or plasmids.
  • Bacterial transformants are validated with antibiotic markers such as ampicillin, kanamycin and streptomycin.
  • In animal and plant cells, a jellyfish fluorescent-protein gene attached to the gene of interest marks successful transformants by fluorescence.

mcqs.q: Why are bacteria the most suitable expression system for recombinant DNA?
options: They have a short generation time and a simple genetic system
They have a long generation time and complex genetics
mcqs.why: Bacteria are most suitable because they have a short generation time and a simple genetic system, and they easily take up recombinant plasmid.

mcqs.q: How are bacterial cells made more permeable so they take up recombinant plasmid?
options: By heating them to 95 degrees C
By bombarding them with metal particles
By treating them with calcium chloride
By injecting them under a microscope
mcqs.why: Bacterial cells easily take up recombinant plasmid especially if treated with calcium chloride to make them more permeable.

mcqs.q: In the cut, copy and paste steps, what happens in the 'cut' step?
options: Multiple copies of the gene are made in bacteria
A gene of interest is removed from a cell using molecular scissors
The gene is inserted into another species
mcqs.why: In the cut step, a gene of interest is removed from the cell of an organism using molecular scissors, before copying and pasting.

mcqs.q: Which organism is named as the regulating system in the 'copy' step?
mcqs.why: Multiple copies are usually made in bacteria, sometimes phage, and the notes name Escherichia coli as the regulating system.

mcqs.q: In micro-injection, where is DNA directly injected in animals?
options: Into the leaf of a plant
Into the nucleus of an egg
mcqs.why: In micro-injection, DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an egg, usually under an optical microscope, to create transgenic species.

mcqs.q: How does electroporation introduce DNA into cells?
options: High-voltage electric shocks increase membrane permeability
DNA-coated particles are fired by a gene gun
A virus carries the DNA into the cell
A liposome encloses the DNA in water
mcqs.why: Electroporation uses high-voltage electric shocks to increase membrane permeability so that DNA can be introduced into cells.

mcqs.q: What is biolistics?
options: Injection of DNA into an egg nucleus
Treatment of bacteria with calcium chloride
Delivery of genes by high-speed particle bombardment into plant cells
mcqs.why: Biolistics delivers nucleic acid into plant cells by high-speed particle bombardment, with DNA-coated metal particles propelled by a gene gun.

mcqs.q: What are liposomes, as used in gene delivery?
options: Small circular DNA molecules in bacteria
Enzymes that cut DNA at specific sites
Minute spherical sacs of molecules enclosing a water droplet
mcqs.why: Liposomes are minute spherical sacs of molecules enclosing a water droplet, and they can carry genes or drugs into cells.

mcqs.q: A bacterial transformant is validated using which kind of marker?
options: An antibiotic such as ampicillin, kanamycin or streptomycin
mcqs.why: For a bacterial clone, an antibiotic is added; if the clone has resistance it stays alive. Markers include ampicillin, kanamycin and streptomycin.

mcqs.q: How are successful transformants identified in animal and plant cells?
options: By fluorescence from a jellyfish fluorescent-protein gene
By the size of their DNA bands on a gel
By their ability to form a callus
mcqs.why: A gene for a fluorescent protein from jellyfish is attached to the gene of interest, so successful cells give fluorescence under certain lighting.

lessons.title: Polymerase Chain Reaction: Components, Mechanism and Applications
lessons.notes_html:
The Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) can create millions of copies of a single gene or any specific small piece of DNA quickly in a test tube. It was originally invented by Kary Mullis in 1983; he received the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 1993. PCR is based on the in vitro replication process and takes its name from the DNA replication enzyme in a cell; it is a chain reaction because polymerase carries out replication over and over again until there are millions of copies of the desired gene (DNA). The book notes that millions of copies of the gene of interest can be obtained after 30 cycles of PCR.

26.1.3 Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)

Components of PCR Technique

  • Template DNA or target DNA — the specific DNA to be copied, e.g. a useful gene, DNA of an infected organism, or DNA for fingerprinting.
  • Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) — four types of free nucleotides, dATP, dGTP, dTTP and dCTP, used as raw material for new DNA.
  • Primers — sequences of about 15-20 bases needed because DNA polymerase cannot start replication itself; they are complementary to the bases on either side of the target DNA. Primers are of two kinds: forward (sense) primers and reverse (antisense) primers.
  • Taq polymerase — a temperature-tolerant (thermostable) enzyme extracted from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus, which lives in hot springs; the book states it can withstand high temperature up to 115°C. PCR is done in an automatic PCR machine or thermocycler, which regulates temperature during the steps.

Mechanism of Polymerase Chain Reaction

Typically, PCR consists of a series of 20-40 repeated temperature and time change cycles, programmed in the thermocycler. Each cycle has three steps:

  • Denaturation (unwinding): The template is heated to 94-95°C for one minute (maximum up to five minutes). The double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) becomes single-stranded (ssDNA), and each strand acts as a template for in vitro DNA synthesis.
  • Primer annealing (hybridization): The forward and backward primers anneal to the single-stranded template DNA at complementary regions, usually at 54-55°C for approximately 1-2 minutes (temperature depends on primer length and sequence).
  • Extension or polymerization: Taq DNA polymerase synthesizes new DNA strands at the 3' ends of the primers using dNTPs, standardized at 72°C and taking one minute. At the end of the first cycle, one target DNA molecule is converted into two daughter molecules; the number of DNA molecules doubles after each cycle, so amplification is exponential.

The Application of Polymerase Chain Reaction

  • To diagnose viral infections, genetic disorders and cancer; PCR is an efficient diagnostic technique for specific infectious agents e.g. HBV, HCV, HIV.
  • To identify criminals in forensic laboratories (DNA fingerprinting); suspect DNA and crime-scene DNA are analysed by PCR.
  • To determine the evolutionary history of human populations — DNA was sequenced from a 76,000-year-old mummified human brain and from a 17 to 20 million-year-old plant fossil after PCR amplification.
  • Detection of micro-organisms in food samples, water and the environment with species-specific primers.
  • Reactions for DNA sequencing; genome analysis and generating markers for genetic and physical maps; RT-PCR (reverse transcriptase-PCR) makes cDNA directly from purified mRNA.
  • Detection of genetic mutations responsible for genetic diseases and cancers, even in embryonic conditions and in sex cells (sperm and egg).

Key Points

  • PCR makes millions of copies of a gene in a test tube; Kary Mullis invented it in 1983 (Nobel Prize 1993).
  • Components: template DNA, dNTPs (dATP, dGTP, dTTP, dCTP), primers of 15-20 bases, and Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus.
  • One cycle: denaturation at 94-95°C, annealing at 54-55°C, extension at 72°C; 20-40 cycles double the DNA each time.
  • Applications: diagnosis (HBV, HCV, HIV), forensics, evolutionary studies, detecting micro-organisms, sequencing and genome analysis.

mcqs.q: Who invented PCR, and in which year?
mcqs.why: The Polymerase Chain Reaction was originally invented by Kary Mullis in 1983; he received the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 1993.

mcqs.q: How many bases long are PCR primers, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: Primers are sequences of about 15-20 bases, needed because DNA polymerase cannot start replication by itself.

mcqs.q: From which bacterium is Taq polymerase extracted?
mcqs.why: Taq polymerase is a thermostable enzyme extracted from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium that lives in hot springs.

mcqs.q: What happens during denaturation in a PCR cycle?
options: Primers bind to the template at 54-55 degrees C
Taq polymerase builds new DNA at 72 degrees C
The DNA is cut by restriction enzymes
The template is heated to 94-95 degrees C and strands part
mcqs.why: In denaturation the template is heated to 94-95 degrees C for about one minute, so double-stranded DNA becomes single-stranded.

mcqs.q: At what temperature does primer annealing usually occur?
mcqs.why: Primer annealing, or hybridization, usually takes place at 54-55 degrees C for approximately 1-2 minutes, depending on primer length and sequence.

mcqs.q: At what temperature does Taq polymerase synthesize new DNA in the extension step?
mcqs.why: Extension or polymerization is standardized at 72 degrees C and takes one minute, with Taq building strands at the 3 prime ends of primers.

mcqs.q: Starting from one target DNA molecule, how many molecules are present after 5 PCR cycles? (Working: copies double each cycle, so 2^5 = 32)
mcqs.why: Amplification is exponential and doubles each cycle: after 5 cycles, 2 to the power 5 = 32 molecules from one starting molecule.

mcqs.q: How many cycles does a typical PCR run, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: PCR typically consists of a series of 20-40 repeated temperature and time change cycles programmed in the thermocycler.

mcqs.q: Which machine regulates temperature during PCR?
mcqs.why: PCR is done in an automatic PCR machine or thermocycler, which regulates temperature during the denaturation, annealing and extension steps.

mcqs.q: Which set of infections can PCR help to diagnose, as listed in the notes?
mcqs.why: PCR is an efficient diagnostic technique for specific infectious agents, and the notes give HBV, HCV and HIV as examples.

lessons.title: Genomic Library, cDNA Library and Locating a Gene with a Probe
lessons.notes_html:
A cloned gene is most useful when it can be stored and found again. A genomic library stores the whole DNA of an organism as a collection of bacterial or bacteriophage clones, and a labelled probe is then used to locate the one clone that carries the gene of interest.

26.1.4 Genomic Library

A genome is a full set of genes or chromosomes of an individual. A genomic library is a collection of bacterial or bacteriophage clones, each clone containing a particular segment of DNA from the source cell. The collection of genomic libraries of different organisms is called a gene bank.

Making a Genomic Library

  • An organism's DNA is sliced into pieces by a molecular scissor (restriction enzyme).
  • The pieces are put into vectors (plasmids or viruses) cut with the same molecular scissor, and the vectors are taken up by host bacteria.
  • The ligase enzyme connects the DNA pieces, now called recombinant DNA.
  • The entire collection of these bacterial or bacteriophage clones contains all the genes of that organism.

Complementary DNA Library (cDNA Library)

The complementary DNA library is the collection of clones of DNA which are complementary copies of mature mRNA (devoid of introns) separated from a particular cell.

How Reverse Transcriptase Helps to Make a Mammalian Gene for Cloning

For a mammalian gene to be expressed in a bacterium, the gene must be accompanied by a proper regulatory region, and the DNA should not contain introns, because bacterial cells do not have the necessary enzymes to process or mature primary mRNA. The enzyme reverse transcriptase is used to make a DNA copy of all the mature mRNA molecules from a cell. This DNA is called complementary DNA (cDNA) and does not contain introns: the gene is transcribed to RNA, introns are removed and exons spliced together for mRNA, the mRNA is isolated and reverse transcriptase synthesizes a DNA strand, the mRNA is digested, and DNA polymerase synthesizes the second strand.

Locating a Gene of Interest with a Particular Probe

A particular probe is a single-stranded nucleotide sequence that will hybridize (pair) into a certain piece of DNA; it is used to search a genetic library for a certain gene. Location of the probe is possible because the probe carries either a radioactive isotope of phosphorus or a fluorescent dye. Steps:

  • Bacterial cells, each carrying a particular DNA fragment, are plated onto agar in a petri dish.
  • The probe is placed on these petri dishes; the probe is made of nine or more nucleotides.
  • The probe hybridizes (forms pairing) into the gene of interest.
  • The gene can be isolated from the fragment.
  • This particular fragment can be cloned further or even analysed for its particular DNA sequence.

Key Points

  • A genome is the full set of genes or chromosomes of an individual.
  • A genomic library is a collection of bacterial or bacteriophage clones covering all the genes of an organism; libraries of different organisms form a gene bank.
  • It is made by cutting DNA and vectors with the same restriction enzyme, joining with ligase, and taking the vectors up into host bacteria.
  • A cDNA library holds complementary copies of mature mRNA, without introns.
  • Reverse transcriptase makes intron-free cDNA from mature mRNA, so mammalian genes can be expressed in bacteria.
  • A labelled probe (radioactive phosphorus or fluorescent dye) hybridizes to and locates the gene of interest in the library.

mcqs.q: What is a genome?
options: A full set of genes or chromosomes of an individual
mcqs.why: A genome is a full set of genes or chromosomes of an individual, and a genomic library stores that DNA as bacterial or bacteriophage clones.

mcqs.q: What is a genomic library?
options: A collection of mature mRNA molecules
A set of primers for PCR
A collection of bacterial or bacteriophage clones, each containing a segment of DNA from the source cell
A bank of antibiotics used for selection
mcqs.why: A genomic library is a collection of bacterial or bacteriophage clones, each clone containing a particular segment of DNA from the source cell.

mcqs.q: What is a collection of genomic libraries of different organisms called?
mcqs.why: The collection of genomic libraries of different organisms is called a gene bank, as stated in the notes for this lesson.

mcqs.q: When making a genomic library, the DNA pieces and the vectors are cut with what?
mcqs.why: The organism's DNA and the vectors are both cut with the same molecular scissor, then joined by ligase and taken up by host bacteria.

mcqs.q: A cDNA library holds complementary copies of what?
mcqs.why: The cDNA library is the collection of clones of DNA that are complementary copies of mature mRNA, separated from a particular cell and devoid of introns.

mcqs.q: Why must a mammalian gene for cloning in bacteria be free of introns?
options: Bacterial cells do not have the enzymes to process or mature primary mRNA
Introns make the gene too short
Bacteria cannot copy any DNA with exons
Introns block the action of ligase only
mcqs.why: Bacterial cells lack the necessary enzymes to process or mature primary mRNA, so the DNA used should not contain introns.

mcqs.q: Which enzyme makes a DNA copy from mature mRNA when preparing a cDNA?
mcqs.why: Reverse transcriptase is used to make a DNA copy of mature mRNA molecules; this intron-free DNA is called complementary DNA, or cDNA.

mcqs.q: After reverse transcriptase makes the first DNA strand from mRNA, what makes the second strand?
options: DNA ligase, after cutting with EcoRI
DNA polymerase, after the mRNA is digested
mcqs.why: The mRNA is digested and DNA polymerase synthesizes the second strand, completing the double-stranded cDNA molecule for cloning.

mcqs.q: What makes a probe's location detectable in a library?
options: It carries a radioactive isotope of phosphorus or a fluorescent dye
It is at least 1000 bases long
It is coated in gold particles
mcqs.why: Location of the probe is possible because the probe carries either a radioactive isotope of phosphorus or a fluorescent dye.

mcqs.q: How long is a probe used to search a library, at minimum?
mcqs.why: The probe placed on the petri dishes is made of nine or more nucleotides and hybridizes into the gene of interest.

lessons.title: DNA Sequencing and Gel Electrophoresis
lessons.notes_html:
DNA sequencing is the process of determining the order of the four chemical building blocks known as 'bases' that make up the DNA molecule. The sequence tells scientists the kind of genetic information carried in a particular segment. One of the important tools used in DNA sequencing techniques is gel electrophoresis.

26.2 DNA Sequencing

26.2.1 Gel Electrophoresis

This laboratory technique is used to separate fragments of DNA, RNA and proteins in an effort to identify their origin. Enzymes chop the long filaments of DNA into fragments of varying size. The fragments are placed into small wells (holes) in a gel made of agarose or polyacrylamide, aligned along one end. The gel is exposed to an electric current, positive on one side and negative on the other. DNA fragment travel is inversely proportional to its length: the biggest, heaviest fragments do not move easily, get stuck close to the wells, and the most (small, highly) charged particles pass through with less difficulty; intermediate particles are distributed in between. In the end, fragments of different sizes leave a banded pattern of DNA on the gel.

Agarose GelPolyacrylamide Gel
Used for relatively large DNA molecules (more than 50 nucleotides)Used for high resolution of short DNA fragments (less than 50 nucleotides)

Visualization of Fragments

To visualize DNA fragments, the gel is stained with DNA-binding fluorescent dyes and viewed under an ultraviolet transilluminator. DNA bands can also be transferred from the gel to a nitrocellulose membrane for autoradiography (X-ray imaging). Thick bands represent a high concentration of same-size fragments, while thin bands exhibit low concentration. If a particular sized fragment is to be used for further analysis, the piece of gel containing that band can be cut and its DNA purified again.

26.2.2 DNA Sequencing Techniques

In the late 1970s, methods were developed that allowed the nucleotide sequence of any purified DNA fragment to be determined simply and quickly. These methods are based upon three steps:

  • To generate pieces of DNA of different sizes, all starting from the same point and ending at a different point.
  • Separation of these different pieces of DNA on agarose gel.
  • Reading of the sequence from the gel.

Horizontal and Vertical Gel Electrophoresis

The book's Fig. 26.6 shows the apparatus in two forms. In horizontal gel electrophoresis, the gel lies flat in a tank of buffer solution, with slots for samples at one end, electrodes at the two ends, and the bands (visible after suitable treatment) moving across the gel in the direction of movement. In vertical gel electrophoresis, the gel stands upright in a plastic frame: sample wells and buffer are at the top, the stacking gel lies above the running gel, the cathode (−) is at the top and the anode (+) at the bottom, with buffer below. In both forms the separated fragments form bands whose position shows their size.

Key Points

  • DNA sequencing determines the order of the four bases in a DNA molecule.
  • Gel electrophoresis separates DNA, RNA and protein fragments; fragment travel is inversely proportional to length.
  • Agarose is for large DNA (more than 50 nucleotides); polyacrylamide gives high resolution for short fragments (less than 50).
  • Bands are visualized with fluorescent dyes under UV, or by autoradiography; thick bands mean high concentration.
  • Sequencing methods rest on three steps: make different-sized pieces, separate them on a gel, and read the sequence.

mcqs.q: What does DNA sequencing determine?
options: The order of the four bases in a DNA molecule
The number of chromosomes in a cell
The size of a whole genome only
The concentration of proteins in blood
mcqs.why: DNA sequencing is the process of determining the order of the four chemical building blocks called bases that make up the DNA molecule.

mcqs.q: How does fragment travel in gel electrophoresis relate to fragment length?
options: Travel is directly proportional to length
Travel does not depend on length
Travel is inversely proportional to length
Only charged fragments move, whatever their length
mcqs.why: DNA fragment travel is inversely proportional to its length: the biggest, heaviest fragments stay close to the wells while small ones pass through easily.

mcqs.q: Which gel is used for relatively large DNA molecules of more than 50 nucleotides?
mcqs.why: Agarose gel is used for relatively large DNA molecules of more than 50 nucleotides, while polyacrylamide suits short fragments.

mcqs.q: Polyacrylamide gel gives high resolution for DNA fragments of what size?
mcqs.why: Polyacrylamide gel is used for high resolution of short DNA fragments, that is, fragments of less than 50 nucleotides.

mcqs.q: How are DNA fragments visualized on a gel?
options: By adding antibiotics to the gel
By staining with DNA-binding fluorescent dyes and viewing under an ultraviolet transilluminator
By heating the gel to 95 degrees C
By washing the gel with calcium chloride
mcqs.why: To visualize DNA fragments, the gel is stained with DNA-binding fluorescent dyes and viewed under an ultraviolet transilluminator.

mcqs.q: What do thick bands on a gel represent?
options: A high concentration of same-size fragments
A low concentration of same-size fragments
mcqs.why: Thick bands represent a high concentration of same-size fragments, while thin bands exhibit a low concentration of such fragments.

mcqs.q: DNA bands can be transferred from a gel to which membrane for autoradiography?
mcqs.why: DNA bands can also be transferred from the gel to a nitrocellulose membrane for autoradiography, which is X-ray imaging.

mcqs.q: DNA sequencing methods rest on three steps. What is the first step?
options: Reading the sequence from the gel
Generating pieces of DNA of different sizes, all starting from the same point
Staining the gel with fluorescent dye
mcqs.why: The first step is to generate pieces of DNA of different sizes, all starting from the same point and ending at a different point.

mcqs.q: In vertical gel electrophoresis, where are the cathode and anode?
options: Cathode at the top, anode at the bottom
Cathode at the bottom, anode at the top
Both electrodes in the buffer below
mcqs.why: In the vertical apparatus the cathode (negative) is at the top and the anode (positive) is at the bottom, with buffer below.

mcqs.q: In horizontal gel electrophoresis, the gel lies how?
options: Flat in a tank of buffer solution
mcqs.why: In horizontal gel electrophoresis the gel lies flat in a tank of buffer solution, with slots for samples at one end and electrodes at the two ends.

lessons.title: Sanger-Coulson, Maxam-Gilbert and Automated DNA Sequencing
lessons.notes_html:
Three methods are generally used to generate DNA fragments of different sizes for sequencing: the Sanger-Coulson method, the Maxam-Gilbert method and automated DNA sequencing (next generation sequencing).

26.2.3 Methods of DNA Sequencing

i) Sanger-Coulson Method / Dideoxy Method

In this method, dideoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (ddNTPs) are used to terminate DNA synthesis at different sites, so it is also called the dideoxy method. It was developed by Frederick Sanger along with Andrew Coulson in 1977; they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1980. It has become the standard because of its practicality and is similar to the natural process of DNA synthesis.

Procedure: Dideoxyribonucleotides are the same as deoxyribonucleotides except they contain a hydrogen group on the 3' carbon instead of a hydroxyl group (OH). When a dideoxyribonucleotide is integrated into a sequence, no phosphodiester bond can form with the next nucleotide, so the DNA chain is terminated. For sequencing, double-stranded DNA is denatured by heat into single strands; the template strand is tagged with a known sequence at its 3' end so a complementary primer can bind. The solution is divided into four tubes labelled 'G', 'A', 'T' and 'C': the 'G' tube gets all four dNTPs, ddGTP and DNA polymerase; the 'A' tube ddATP; the 'T' tube ddTTP; the 'C' tube ddCTP. Normal free A, T, G and C nucleotides and Taq polymerase are also present, and the tubes are placed in a PCR machine. Whenever a dideoxynucleotide is incorporated, a chain-terminating event occurs — e.g. in the ddTTP tube, only fragments terminating on 'T' are produced. All reactions start from the same nucleotide and end with a specific base, so bands of all different lengths are produced. The DNA is denatured again and the contents of each tube are run in separate lanes on a polyacrylamide gel; the gel is exposed to UV light or X-rays, depending on the labelling method, and the sequence is read.

ii) Maxam-Gilbert Method

This method was developed by Allan Maxam and Walter Gilbert (1976-77). It is also known as the chemical cleavage method because it is based on chemical modification of DNA and subsequent cleavage at specific bases.

Procedure: The DNA to be sequenced must denature so the two strands separate; one strand is purified and divided into four samples (G, A+G, T+C and C). Each sample is treated with modified chemical reagents and cleavage reagents: the former chemically modify the nucleotides they are specific for, making them susceptible to cleavage, while the latter cut the DNA strand at specific points. For example, in the 'G' sample the fragment is cleaved from all points where G is present; in 'A+G' from A as well as G, and so on. The products are run through gel electrophoresis and the sequence is finally read from the autoradiograph of the gel pattern.

iii) Automated DNA Sequencing

Automatic sequencing machines have greatly improved the quality and speed of sequencing; the basic principle is the same as manual sequencing except for a few differences. There is no need for radiolabelling and autoradiography: fluorescently labelled ddNTPs make reading easy, convenient and automatic with UV laser detectors. Each of the four types of ddNTPs can be labelled with a specific dye, so a specific colour is attributed to a particular nucleotide or base. After electrophoresis, the computer reads the sequence: laser beams excite the fluorescent dyes, which emit specific spectral waves (coloured light) recorded by a photoelectric device; the data is fed to a computer, converted into the nucleotide sequence, and also represented as specific peaks indicating each nitrogen base.

Sanger-Coulson MethodMaxam-Gilbert Method
Enzymatic: DNA synthesis with ddNTPs terminates the chainChemical: bases are chemically modified, then the DNA is cleaved at those bases
Four tubes, each with one ddNTP (ddGTP, ddATP, ddTTP, ddCTP)Four samples: G, A+G, T+C, C
Developed by Sanger and Coulson, 1977Developed by Maxam and Gilbert, 1976-77

Key Points

  • Sanger-Coulson (1977, Nobel Prize 1980) uses ddNTPs, which lack the 3'-OH group, to terminate chains — the dideoxy method.
  • Four tubes (G, A, T, C), gel lanes and band order give the sequence in the Sanger method.
  • Maxam-Gilbert (1976-77) is the chemical cleavage method, with four samples: G, A+G, T+C and C.
  • Automated sequencing uses fluorescently labelled ddNTPs, UV laser detectors and a computer, with no radiolabelling or autoradiography.
  • In automated sequencing each base has its own dye colour and is shown as a peak.

mcqs.q: The Sanger-Coulson method is also called what, and why?
options: The dideoxy method, because ddNTPs terminate DNA synthesis
The chemical cleavage method, because chemicals cut the DNA
The automated method, because computers read the DNA
The hybridization method, because probes pair with DNA
mcqs.why: It is called the dideoxy method because dideoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (ddNTPs) are used to terminate DNA synthesis at different sites.

mcqs.q: Who developed the Sanger-Coulson method, and in which year?
mcqs.why: The method was developed by Frederick Sanger along with Andrew Coulson in 1977; they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1980.

mcqs.q: How does a dideoxyribonucleotide differ from a normal deoxyribonucleotide?
options: It has an extra phosphate group
It has a hydrogen group on the 3 prime carbon instead of a hydroxyl group
It contains uracil instead of thymine
It has no nitrogen base at all
mcqs.why: Dideoxyribonucleotides contain a hydrogen group on the 3 prime carbon instead of a hydroxyl (OH) group, so no phosphodiester bond can form next.

mcqs.q: What happens when a dideoxynucleotide is incorporated into a growing DNA chain?
options: The chain grows twice as fast
The primer falls off and restarts
mcqs.why: When a dideoxyribonucleotide is integrated, no phosphodiester bond can form with the next nucleotide, so the DNA chain is terminated.

mcqs.q: In the Sanger method, the reaction mixture is divided into how many tubes, labelled how?
options: Three tubes labelled G, A and T
Four tubes labelled G, A, T and C
Four tubes labelled G, A+G, T+C and C
Two tubes labelled sense and antisense
mcqs.why: The solution is divided into four tubes labelled G, A, T and C, each receiving all four dNTPs, DNA polymerase and one kind of ddNTP.

mcqs.q: The Maxam-Gilbert method is also known as what?
mcqs.why: Maxam-Gilbert is also known as the chemical cleavage method because it is based on chemical modification of DNA and subsequent cleavage at specific bases.

mcqs.q: Into which four samples is DNA divided in the Maxam-Gilbert method?
mcqs.why: In Maxam-Gilbert, one purified strand is divided into four samples: G, A+G, T+C and C, each treated with modification and cleavage reagents.

mcqs.q: In automated DNA sequencing, what replaces radiolabelling and autoradiography?
options: Fluorescently labelled ddNTPs read by UV laser detectors
mcqs.why: Automated sequencing uses fluorescently labelled ddNTPs, making reading easy and automatic with UV laser detectors, with no radiolabelling or autoradiography.

mcqs.q: In automated sequencing, how is each base distinguished?
options: Each of the four ddNTPs is labelled with a specific dye colour
Each base runs in a separate test tube only
Each base is cut by a different restriction enzyme
Each base is shown by band thickness alone
mcqs.why: Each of the four types of ddNTPs can be labelled with a specific dye, so a specific colour is attributed to a particular nucleotide or base.

mcqs.q: After electrophoresis in automated sequencing, the computer represents each base as what?
options: A thick or thin band only
A specific peak indicating each nitrogen base
A radioactive spot on X-ray film
mcqs.why: Laser-excited dyes emit coloured light recorded by a photoelectric device; the data is converted into the sequence and shown as specific peaks for each base.

lessons.title: DNA Analysis, DNA Fingerprinting and RFLPs
lessons.notes_html:
The process of matching an unknown sample of DNA with a known sample to see if they correspond is called DNA profiling. It is also called DNA fingerprinting because of its similarity to identifying fingerprints (the techniques are very different; it is also called DNA testing / DNA typing). If, after separation by gel electrophoresis, the band patterns of two samples are identical, both must have come from the same individual; if the pattern is similar, the two individuals are probably related. Forensic scientists use it to identify individuals by their nucleotide sequence. The first DNA fingerprint was made by Alec Jeffreys (the book prints 'Alec Jeffrey'), an English geneticist, in 1985.

26.3 DNA Analysis

26.3.1 Use / Applications / Purposes of DNA Analysis

  • DNA fingerprinting in paternity suits, when the identity of someone's biological father needs to be known for legal reasons, and establishment of paternity and other family relationships.
  • At a crime scene, forensic specialists collect samples such as blood or semen, which contain DNA.
  • To identify crime and catastrophe victims.
  • To match organ donors with recipients in transplant programs.
  • To detect bacteria and other micro-organisms that pollute water, air, food and soil.

26.3.2 Procedure / Mechanism of DNA Analysis

One of the most important methods is restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP), pronounced 'Riflips' — the different-sized fragments of DNA produced by a particular restriction enzyme. The book's extra information notes that humans share about 98% of their genes with chimpanzees, 92% with mice, 76% with zebrafish, 51% with fruit fly and 18% with E. coli bacteria.

1. Collection of DNA samples: A very small fraction of DNA is sufficient, because it can be copied several times with PCR. DNA can be collected even from a drop of blood, a cell of a single hair root, or a single sperm. DNA samples can also be collected from mummified organisms or fossils when evolutionary relationships are to be studied.

Placement of RFLPs: Every person has a unique set of RFLPs, because the restriction site of a particular enzyme is always different in number and distribution in all humans on earth except monozygotic twins. Humans have 99% similarity in the nucleotide sequence of their genomes; the 1% difference establishes the individuality of every person. Placement of RFLPs is the digestion of DNA samples by a particular restriction enzyme, producing a set of different-sized DNA fragments.

Separation of RFLPs: The DNA fragments are electrophoresed on agarose gel, and the mixture of RFLPs is loaded in polyacrylamide gel and run for electrophoresis. Fragments of various lengths move at different rates from the negative to the positive pole within the gel; when movement is stopped, the gel is treated further to observe the banding pattern.

Southern Blotting

This method was invented by British biologist Edwin Southern. A Southern blot is routinely used for detection of a specific DNA sequence in DNA samples. Southern blotting combines transfer of electrophoresis-separated DNA fragments to a filter membrane with subsequent fragment detection by probe hybridization: the double-stranded fragments separated by electrophoresis are denatured to single-stranded fragments, transferred from gel to membrane, covered with a radioactively labelled probe in single-strand form and incubated; excess probe is washed off.

Autoradiography

After hybridization, excess probes are washed from the membrane, and the pattern of hybridization is visualized on X-ray film by exposing the membrane to an X-ray source. This technique is known as autoradiography. The banding pattern originally obtained in the gel due to separation of RFLPs is now developed on an X-ray film.

Key Points

  • DNA profiling / fingerprinting matches an unknown DNA sample with a known one; identical band patterns mean the same individual.
  • First DNA fingerprint: Alec Jeffreys, 1985.
  • Uses: paternity, crime-scene evidence, identifying victims, organ-donor matching, and detecting polluting micro-organisms.
  • RFLPs are different-sized fragments from one restriction enzyme; they are unique to each person except monozygotic twins (99% of the human genome is shared, 1% differs).
  • Steps: collect DNA (even a drop of blood or one hair root), digest to RFLPs, separate by electrophoresis, Southern blotting, then autoradiography on X-ray film.

mcqs.q: Matching an unknown DNA sample with a known sample to see if they correspond is called what?
mcqs.why: The process of matching an unknown sample of DNA with a known sample is called DNA profiling, also called DNA fingerprinting, testing or typing.

mcqs.q: Who made the first DNA fingerprint, and in which year?
mcqs.why: The first DNA fingerprint was made by Alec Jeffreys, an English geneticist, in 1985, as recorded in the notes for this lesson.

mcqs.q: If two samples give identical band patterns after gel electrophoresis, what does that mean?
options: The two individuals are probably related
Both samples must have come from the same individual
The restriction enzyme failed to cut
mcqs.why: If the band patterns of two samples are identical, both must have come from the same individual; a similar pattern suggests the individuals are probably related.

mcqs.q: RFLP is pronounced 'Riflips'. What does it stand for in meaning?
options: The order of bases in a DNA molecule
A labelled probe used in libraries
The different-sized fragments of DNA produced by a particular restriction enzyme
mcqs.why: Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) refers to the different-sized fragments of DNA produced by a particular restriction enzyme.

mcqs.q: According to the book's extra information, about what percentage of genes do humans share with chimpanzees?
mcqs.why: The book's extra information notes that humans share about 98 percent of their genes with chimpanzees, 92 percent with mice and 76 percent with zebrafish.

mcqs.q: Every person has a unique set of RFLPs, except for whom?
mcqs.why: RFLPs are unique because restriction sites differ in number and distribution in all humans on earth except monozygotic twins.

mcqs.q: How much of the human genome is similar between people, and how much differs?
mcqs.why: Humans have 99 percent similarity in the nucleotide sequence of their genomes; the 1 percent difference establishes the individuality of every person.

mcqs.q: How little DNA can be enough for DNA analysis?
options: A whole litre of blood is needed
A drop of blood, a cell of a single hair root, or a single sperm
Only DNA from living tissue can be used
mcqs.why: A very small fraction of DNA is sufficient because it can be copied with PCR; DNA can come from a drop of blood, a single hair root cell or a single sperm.

mcqs.q: Who invented Southern blotting?
mcqs.why: Southern blotting was invented by British biologist Edwin Southern and is routinely used for detection of a specific DNA sequence in DNA samples.

mcqs.q: In DNA analysis, the hybridization pattern is visualized on X-ray film by which technique?
mcqs.why: After hybridization and washing, the pattern is visualized on X-ray film by exposing the membrane to an X-ray source; this technique is autoradiography.

lessons.title: Genome Maps and the Human Genome Project
lessons.notes_html:
The gene is the basic unit of biological information; hereditary characteristics pass from parents to offspring through genes in their gametes. The collection of all the genes found in one complete set of chromosomes is called the genome. The haploid organism, or egg and sperm, has one copy of the genome, while a diploid organism (cell) contains two copies. The book compares the human genome to a book with 23 units (chromosomes), each with several thousand stories (genes), made of paragraphs called exons interrupted by introns, written in letters called bases — thymine, guanine, cytosine and adenine (TGCA).

26.4 Genome Maps

Genome Analyses

For the study of the genomes of various organisms, a new sub-branch of biotechnology has been created called genomics, which deals with exploration and analysis of the complete DNA sequence of an organism's genome. The genome of Haemophilus influenzae was published in 1995. Frederick Sanger also sequenced the first bacteriophage genome.

Genome Maps

Genome analysis helps develop two broad categories of maps:

Genetic MapsPhysical Maps
Exhibit the sequence (order) of gene loci along the length of DNAPhysical mapping finds the order and physical distance between DNA base pairs by DNA markers

Physical mapping can determine the sequence of DNA base pairs with high accuracy.

Genetic Markers

Genetic maps have landmarks called genetic markers, which contain variable numbers of tandem repeats (short tandem repeats and single nucleotide polymorphism). Genetic markers are useful for generating genetic maps when there are occasional, predictable mutations during meiosis; over many generations these lead to a high degree of variability in the DNA content of the marker from individual to individual.

26.4.1 Human Genome Project (HGP)

In 1990, an international cooperative venture called the Human Genome Project (HGP) set out to sequence the complete human genome — a catalogue of the bases A, T, C and G in human DNA. The project was originally founded by the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Institutes of Health, which established the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI). Its first director was James D. Watson; later the institute was led by Dr Francis Collins (the book prints 'Collin'). The 'Wellcome Trust' of the UK became a major partner, with additional contributions from China, France, Japan, Germany and others. In 2003, the project announced it had succeeded: the human genome comprises 3.22 billion nucleotides and approximately 20,000 to 25,000 genes. Note: the unit's exercise rounds the genome size to 3 billion nucleotides.

26.4.2 Major Goals of Human Genome Project

  • To identify all the approximately 20,000 to 25,000 genes in the human genome.
  • To determine the sequences of the chemical base pairs that make up human DNA, about 3.22 billion.
  • To store this information in databases.
  • To improve tools for data analysis.
  • To transfer related technologies to the private sector, and address the ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI) that may arise from the project.

Benefits of HGP — Molecular Medicine

  • Improved diagnosis of diseases.
  • Earlier detection of genetic predisposition to certain diseases.
  • Rational drug design.
  • Gene therapy and control systems for drugs.
  • Pharmacogenomics — the study of how genes affect a person's response to drugs.

Key Points

  • The genome is all the genes in one complete set of chromosomes; genomics studies complete genome sequences.
  • Genetic maps show the order of gene loci; physical maps show order and distance in base pairs using DNA markers.
  • Genetic markers include short tandem repeats and single nucleotide polymorphisms.
  • HGP (1990-2003), first directed by James D. Watson, sequenced the human genome: 3.22 billion nucleotides, about 20,000-25,000 genes.
  • HGP goals included identifying all genes, storing data, improving analysis tools, technology transfer and addressing ELSI.
  • Benefits lie in molecular medicine: better diagnosis, early detection, rational drug design, gene therapy and pharmacogenomics.

lessons.title: Tissue Culture and Plant Tissue Culture Methods
lessons.notes_html:
Tissue culture is the growth of a tissue in an artificial liquid culture medium. In 1902, the German botanist Gottlieb Haberlandt revealed that plant cells are totipotent — each cell has the full genetic potential of the organism, so a single cell could become a complete plant. In 1958, the British botanist F.C. Steward grew a complete carrot plant from a tiny piece of phloem, providing sugars, minerals and vitamins and adding coconut milk (later found to contain the plant hormone cytokinin). The cultured cells divided and produced a callus (an undifferentiated group of cells), which later differentiated into shoot and root and developed into complete plants.

26.5 Tissue Culture

The initial plant part used to develop tissue culture is known as an explant; it may be a single cell (protoplast), a piece of tissue, or a complete organ (seed, leaf or twig). On this basis, tissue culture is called cell culture or organ culture. Plantlets are the young plants developed during tissue culture, and micro-propagation is the production of a large number of plants from small plant material.

Somatic embryogenesis is an artificial process in which a plant or embryo is derived from a single somatic cell; somatic embryos form from ordinary plant tissue not normally involved in embryo development, and no endosperm or seed coat forms around a somatic embryo. Plants produced from tissue culture are genetically identical to the original plant, so they are called soma clones; however, genetic variation is sometimes observed among progeny of plants regenerated from somatic cells cultured in vitro — this is called soma clonal variation.

Cell CultureOrgan Culture
Cells are artificially grown under laboratory conditions (in vitro)Culture of isolated organs such as root, stem, anther, etc.; named after the organ used

26.5.1 Methods of Tissue Culture

Methods are based on the type of explant used: meristem, anther, ovary, embryo, callus and suspension culture, etc.

Meristem culture: Meristems are tissues of undifferentiated cells capable of rapid division; culture using meristems is meristem culture. With the correct proportions of auxins and cytokinin added to a liquid medium, many new shoots develop from a single shoot tip, and when these are removed more shoots form. Meristem culture has led to micro-propagation — the commercial production of thousands, even millions, of identical seedlings in limited space. Its advantage is that the plants are germ free (devoid of viruses), because meristems lack a vascular system, which is the main route for viruses travelling through the body. Note: the book mentions a 'single root tip' in one sentence and a 'single shoot tip' in the next; the shoots develop from the shoot tip.

Anther culture technique: Anthers are cultured in a medium containing vitamins and growth regulators; the haploid cells within the pollen grains divide, producing pro-embryos of as many as 20-40 cells. When the pollen grains rupture, haploid embryos are released. The experimenter can generate a haploid plant, or add a chemical agent to encourage chromosomal doubling; after doubling, the plants are diploid but homozygous for all their alleles. Anther culture is a direct way to produce plants that express recessive alleles.

Callus CultureCell Suspension Culture
Callus is formed by proliferation of the parent tissue; its cells are parenchymatous, amorphous and unorganized; culturing callus in an appropriate medium is callus culture, which can initiate cell suspensionsRapidly growing cultures are cut into small pieces and shaken in a liquid nutrient medium so single cells or small clumps break off and form a suspension; these cells produce the same chemicals as the entire plant

Cell suspension cultures of Cinchona ledgeriana produce quinine and those of Digitalis lanata produce digitoxin. Scientists imagine cell suspension cultures will be maintained in bioreactors to produce chemicals for drugs, cosmetics and agricultural chemicals.

Protoplast culture: A plant cell with its cell wall removed is a protoplast, commonly isolated from leaf mesophyll cells or cell suspensions. Protoplast culture can develop a whole plant by somatic embryogenesis (synthetic embryos from somatic cells); genetic variation can be induced in these embryos by chemical or physical mutagens — soma clonal variations. Protoplasts are also ideal targets for transformation.

Embryo culture: The culture of mature embryos; zygote or seed embryos are often used as explants, and the embryo develops properly when nourishing tissues (endosperms) were present in the seed during development.

Ovary culture: An in vitro technique in which an unpollinated flower is grown on a suitable nutrient medium to grow new haploid plants; this process of ovary culture is called gynogenesis, and the ovary can regenerate into a fully differentiated plant.

Key Points

  • Tissue culture grows tissue in an artificial medium; plant cells are totipotent (Haberlandt, 1902; Steward's carrot, 1958).
  • Explant is the starting plant part; callus is the undifferentiated cell mass; plantlets are the young plants produced.
  • Micro-propagation makes many plants from small material; tissue-culture plants are soma clones, and variation among them is soma clonal variation.
  • Meristem culture gives virus-free plants; anther culture gives haploid plants that can be doubled to homozygous diploids.
  • Callus culture grows an unorganized callus; suspension cultures of Cinchona make quinine and of Digitalis make digitoxin.
  • Other methods: protoplast culture, embryo culture, and ovary culture (gynogenesis) for haploid plants.

lessons.title: Animal Cell Culture: Techniques and Applications
lessons.notes_html:
Animal cells can also be cultured in artificial media, but unlike plant and bacterial cells, these cells can grow only for a limited number of generations. Growth also depends on the source tissue: some cells cannot divide and grow, e.g. nerve cells and lens cells, while others can repeatedly divide and grow for a limited generation, e.g. fibroblasts. Cultured animal cells are used in recombinant DNA technology, industrial processes (vaccine, monoclonal antibody and drug production), genetic manipulation and cancer research, etc.

26.5.2 Methods of Animal Cell Culture

Techniques of Animal Cell Culture

Plastic containers are used to culture animal cells. A cell culture initiated by cells isolated from a tissue or an animal's organ is known as primary cell culture. If a primary culture is subcultured in fresh media, it establishes secondary cultures, called a secondary culture or cell line.

  • Organ culture — culture of native tissue that retains most of the in vivo histological features.
  • Histotypic culture — culture of cells for their reaggregation to form a tissue-like structure.
  • Organotypic culture — culture of different cell types to form a tissue or organ.

A special incubator is needed for animal cell culture, maintaining the level of carbon dioxide, oxygen, temperature and all other necessary substances. There are two patterns of animal cell growth:

Anchorage DependenceAnchorage Independence
An increase in proliferation seen when cells are allowed to attach to a solid surfaceA cell maintains its capacity to spread, divide and function despite the absence of a stable or inert surface to anchor with

Applications of Animal / Tissue Culture

  • Produce antiviral vaccines and pharmaceutical drugs using cell lines.
  • Amniocentesis — chromosomal analysis of the fetus for various diseases.
  • Produce monoclonal antibodies required from cell lines in culture.
  • Helpful to study the function of cell neurons.
  • Use of artificial skin.
  • Culture tumour cells, to know whether a tumour is benign or cancerous.
  • To know the effects of toxins and pollutants using cell lines.

Note: on one page the book prints 'monoclonal antibiotics' in a list of cultured-cell uses; from the rest of the unit (Sections 26.5.2 applications and 26.7.2) this is monoclonal antibodies.

The unit's summary restates the key definition: a cell culture which is initiated by the cells removed from an animal's organ is called a primary cell culture. The main limitation running through this section is lifespan — unlike bacteria, cultured animal cells divide only for a limited generation, and some, such as nerve and lens cells, do not divide at all, which limits how long a culture can be maintained and used.

Key Points

  • Animal cells grow only for limited generations; nerve and lens cells do not divide, fibroblasts divide for a limited generation.
  • Primary culture comes directly from tissue or organ; subculturing it gives secondary cultures or cell lines.
  • Organ culture retains in vivo features; histotypic culture reaggregates cells into tissue-like structures; organotypic culture combines different cell types.
  • Animal culture needs a special incubator controlling CO₂, oxygen and temperature; growth is anchorage dependent or independent.
  • Applications: vaccines and drugs, amniocentesis, monoclonal antibodies, neuron study, artificial skin, tumour study, and testing toxins and pollutants.
